### Where a dragged layer lands (CAN-47)

Dragging a selected layer shows an empty dashed outline where it would land, and the layouts around it reflow around it,
while a picture of it is carried (see "How dragged things move", above). Where it lands follows the pointer:

- **The slot under the pointer.** In a grid or a wrapping row, the line of children the pointer is on comes first (the
  row it's over, or the nearer one in the gap between rows), then, along that line, the layer goes before the first
  child whose middle is past the pointer, or after the line's last child. Below the last line it goes last. A row or
  column that doesn't wrap goes by the middles along it, wherever the pointer is across it, as before. So in the
  dashboard's four stat cards, Users dragged right past the middle of Open issues gives Revenue, Issues, Users, Uptime,
  and Issues dragged left past the middle of Revenue gives Issues, Revenue, Users, Uptime. Grids that flow by columns,
  and wrapping columns, work the same way turned on their side. A layout that runs backwards goes the way it's drawn: in
  a right-to-left grid or row, or a reversed row or column, "past the middle" is leftwards or upwards, and the slot's
  line stands on the child's right or below it; with lines that wrap upwards (`wrap-reverse`), or a wrapping column in a
  right-to-left page, the lines follow one another up or leftwards, and the end is above or left of the last.
- **Measured from the layout as it was when the drag began.** The dragged layer is hidden and its copy shown somewhere
  else, so what's on screen moves under the pointer. Targets are found in the boxes measured just before the layer is
  hidden: a neighbour that slid into the dragged layer's place isn't under the pointer, and the slots don't move when
  the copy moves. Another frame, or another design, is measured the first time the pointer is over it, before a copy is
  shown in it. Points are mapped back into each frame's first measure, so zooming or panning mid-drag still lands right.
- **A layer stays in the layout it's dragged in while the pointer is over it.** It changes places with its neighbours
  and never drops into one, or into anything inside one, even when the neighbour is a layout, as each of the dashboard's
  revenue bars is. Outside its own layout it goes into the deepest layout under the pointer, as before, in this design
  or another. To put a layer inside its neighbour, press Ctrl as you drag (below), or drag it there in Layers.
- **Ctrl pressed during the drag drops into the layout under the pointer** (PAR-206), Cmd on a Mac: the deepest one
  there, even a neighbour of the layer or a layout inside one, in the slot under the pointer. Letting Ctrl go puts the
  layer back among its neighbours, and the outline follows either way, without the pointer moving. Ctrl held from the
  press doesn't count, since it picked the deepest layer to drag (see "Selecting what you point at"), so Ctrl-dragging a
  stat card still changes places with the others; let it go and press it again to drop into a neighbour. A layer never
  goes into itself or anything inside it. This is Figma's key for changing what a drag nests into, the other way round:
  Figma nests by default and Ctrl stops it, while here a drag stays among its neighbours, as CAN-47 settled, and Ctrl
  nests. Penpot nests whatever a layer is dragged over, with no key to choose.
- **The outline is round a hidden copy of the layer, laid out as the layer is.** A frame draws a layer that has no
  classes from rules about its node alone, so the copy is drawn from those rules too, taken from the frame the layer is
  in, even in another design. The copy carries the node under another attribute, so nothing that finds layers in a frame
  (hit testing, outlines, measuring) takes it for one.
- **Into another design, the copies are what the frame shows** (PAR-464): the state being edited, the variant options
  the board shows, the frame's viewport and the values bound params show, keeping only the bindings the destination has
  params for, as a paste does (see "Copy, paste and paste style").
- **Edge cases.** Children that aren't drawn (hidden in this state) aren't slots; a layer placed after them goes after
  them. A move that leaves the order as it was changes nothing and adds no undo step. An absolutely placed layer doesn't
  reorder; it moves by its insets (below).

Code: the rules are in `@parity-app/editor` (PAR-33), from measures the canvas passes in:
`packages/editor/src/drop-slot.ts` (`slotAt`, geometry only, and `flowOf`, the one reading of a layout's flow that
dropping, dragging and nudging share since PAR-205), `drop-target.ts` (`frameLayout` keeps what was measured, and
`dropTargetAt` finds the layout and slot, and the line marking it) and `move-layers.ts` (`moveLayersWithin` and
`moveLayersAcross`). The app's `apps/desktop/src/renderer/canvas/drop-target.ts` measures (`DragLayouts` reads a frame's
layers' boxes through `frame.ts`'s `nodeBox`, and each layout's flow from its computed style, and `dropInFrame` passes
them in), and `canvas/layer-drag.ts` follows the pointer (`pressLayers` measures when the drag begins; `moveTarget`
finds the frame under the pointer; `DropPreview` shows the copy; `moveLayers` applies the move to the document and the
selection). Whether Ctrl asks for a neighbour is `intoNeighbour` in `drop-target.ts`, which `pressLayers` asks at each
move, and as Ctrl goes down or up, passing `into` on to `dropTargetAt`.

### Moving an absolutely placed layer by dragging (CAN-47)

A layer placed absolutely moves by its insets, live, as the pointer moves (PAR-174): in half steps of the spacing scale,
except along an axis where it snaps (see "Snapping layers while moving and resizing", below). Its outline and size label
follow it. Escape takes the move back, leaving nothing to undo, and a drag that ends where it began adds no undo step.

- **Both sides.** Along each axis it moves by the side it's placed from: the left (or top), unless only the right (or
  bottom) is set. A layer stretched between both sides moves both, so it keeps its size: Calendar's Review slot, placed
  at left 0 and right 0, dragged 24px right is left 6 and right -6.
- **Negative and token insets.** A negative inset is kept, and an inset can go negative. A side set to a length token,
  or left unset, moves from where the frame drew it when the drag began, so it doesn't jump to the parent's edge; once
  moved it's a number of steps, since a token can't be offset. An axis the layer doesn't move along keeps what's
  written, tokens included.

This is the same rule nudging uses, one function for both. Code: `packages/editor/src/move-resize.ts`
(`@parity-app/editor`): `shiftInsets` moves the insets, and `absoluteDrag` follows one drag, taking the layer's style as
the board shows it, where its sides are drawn and what it snaps to, and giving the insets for each pointer move, in half
steps or, where it snapped, to the half pixel. `apps/desktop/src/renderer/canvas/layer-drag.ts` (`followAbsolute`)
measures those from one reading of the frame (`frameGeometry`, PAR-967), its scale and where the sides are drawn
(`insetSteps` in `canvas/layer-measure.ts`), and writes each move in the drag's gesture, one undo step (PAR-441), taking
them back to the drag's checkpoint (`Drag.revert`, from `canvas/gesture.ts`'s `followPress`) on Escape or when the layer
comes back to where it began.

Tests: `packages/editor/src/move-resize.test.ts`, moving: by the side it's placed from, both sides of a stretched layer
(the Review slot), negative insets kept and going negative, half steps, tokens and unset sides from where they're drawn
(a negative side with a token on the other), and an axis with a token that isn't drawn staying put; and dragging the
Review slot, in half steps where nothing is near, exactly where its bottom locks to Lunch's top, 8.25 steps to a line
off the scale, and by the pointer when it isn't drawn. `canvas/layer-measure.test.ts`: the same steps dragged and
snapped from what a frame measured at four scales. End to end (PAR-202), `apps/desktop/e2e/moving.e2e.ts` (2) drags
Calendar's Review slot 24px right to left 6 and right -6, and, with left -2 and both right and top set to the `spacing`
token, 16px right with Ctrl held to left 2 and right -3, with top still `spacing` and the width unchanged. Moving live
and Escape are covered under "Snapping layers while moving and resizing".

Gaps: none known. Dragging itself was first checked by hand, as the end-to-end test now does it.

### A component placed between both edges (PAR-899)

An absolutely placed component or instance with a left and a right inset and no width spans between them, as an element
with no width of its own does in CSS; with a top and a bottom and no height, it spans those too. A component's root
often brings its own size in its classes, such as a separator's `w-full`, which would win over the insets and run it
past its parent, so the layer's style writes `width: auto` (or `height: auto`) over it. A width or height the layer sets
keeps it at that size. Layouts and text span between their insets already, and an image or a video keeps the size of its
picture unless it's given one.

Code: `stretchBetweenEdges` in `packages/style-schema/src/declare.ts`, which `packages/core/src/render.ts` draws as the
component's inline style, over its own.

Tests: `packages/style-schema/src/declare.test.ts`, declarations: a component placed against all four sides writing an
auto width and height, and one with a width keeping it. `packages/core/src/render.test.ts`, sizing: a separator whose
own style is `width: 100%`, placed at left 14 and right 0, drawn `width: auto` between them.

Gaps: none known. Checked in an isolated copy of the app on 2026-11-11: a Separator placed at left 14, right 0 in an
80-step layout was drawn from 56px in to the layout's right edge, 264px wide, where it had run past it.

### Resize handles (CAN-47)

A selected layer has square handles on its corners and invisible strips along its sides, as in Figma, and a selected
design has them on its frames' right and bottom.

- **A handle changes only its own sizes.** The left and right handles change the width, the top and bottom ones the
  height, and a corner both. Nothing changes until the pointer has moved four pixels along the handle's own axes, so a
  click, a double-click or a side's handle dragged along its side changes nothing. Dragging the right handle of the
  dashboard's New project button 50px right made it 196 by 32 with Height still Auto, where it used to set Height to
  Fill.
- **Fill.** A layer in a layout takes a size in whole spacing steps, or fill when its edge comes back to the inside of
  its parent after leaving it. An edge that starts there, as New project's right edge does at the end of its row, gets a
  fixed size until it has been away. Shift keeps the size fixed, and on a corner keeps the proportions. A size along the
  direction of the layout the layer is in takes away `grow`, the older way to fill along it.
- **Absolutely placed layers** keep the opposite edge where it was. The left or top handle moves that inset with the
  edge, so the right or bottom stays put; a layer stretched between both sides changes the dragged side's inset alone,
  keeping both sides; a layer placed from the right or bottom alone moves that inset when its right or bottom handle is
  dragged. Negative and token insets follow the moving rules above, and a side that doesn't move keeps its token. They
  never fill. Their dragged edges snap (PAR-174, "Snapping layers while moving and resizing", below), unless Shift keeps
  a corner's proportions.
- **A frame** takes a width and a height in whole pixels for its viewport, at least 160 by 80. Within 6 screen pixels of
  its viewport's width the width is left unset, so it follows the viewport again; a frame that hugged its content when
  the drag began goes back to hugging it the same way, and one with a height of its own keeps one.
- **A double-click** on a handle makes a layer's size on its axes hug its content, and Alt+double-click makes it fill
  its parent (PAR-169, below); a frame goes back to its viewport's width or its content's height.
- **The hint** ("Drag to resize") closes when a handle is pressed and stays closed through the drag and after it, until
  the pointer next rests on a handle.
- **Small layers keep their middle** (PAR-193). Along an axis where a layer is under 24 screen pixels, its handles sit
  just outside it: the corners and the top and bottom strips above and below a layer that's short, the corners and the
  side strips beside one that's narrow, with the strips running its whole length. So a press anywhere on a layer small
  both ways drags it; one small along only one axis keeps its other axis's strips on it. New project at 50% is 16px
  high: its corners, top and bottom sit above and below it, and only its left and right strips, 4px into each end as on
  any wide layer, are on it. A layer 24px or more keeps its handles on its edges.
- **Escape takes a resize back** (PAR-193), a layer's or a frame's: everything the drag wrote is undone without leaving
  a step to undo or clearing what Redo had, the layer stays selected, and the release that follows does nothing. Escape
  goes to the resize alone, not to the canvas, where it would select the parent. Only the resized design goes back:
  another file an agent changed during the drag, or another design in the same file, keeps its change and its undo step.
  Such a change clears Redo, as any new step does, so Redo comes back only when nothing else changed during the drag.
- **The cursor** shows the handle's arrows wherever the pointer goes during the drag, over the canvas, the frames and
  the panels, until it ends (see "Cursors and Escape during a gesture", below).
- **It starts from what the frame shows** (PAR-464): the layer's style and its layout's direction with the state being
  edited, the variant options the board shows and the frame's viewport, so a layer a variant or a mobile patch places
  absolutely resizes by its insets there, and a row the board shows is a row. The edit still lands where every edit does
  (see "Edits in the state and variant shown").

Code: the rules are `packages/editor/src/move-resize.ts` (`@parity-app/editor`). `resizeStart` reads the layer and its
layout as the board shows them. `layerResize` follows one drag of a layer's handle and gives the style for each pointer
move: `resizeGesture` gives steps or fill, or the insets `resizeInsets` moves for an absolutely placed layer, and
`layerResize` adds the snapped edges and takes `grow` away. `frameResize` follows a frame's, with its snap-back and
smallest size, `layerSizeReset` and `frameSizeReset` are a double-click's, and `edgeAxes` says which sizes a handle
changes. `packages/editor/src/handles.ts` (`handleBoxes`) says where each handle goes. In the app,
`canvas/ResizeHandles.tsx` draws the handles and their hint, which `chrome/Hint.tsx` lets a caller open and close, and
`canvas/CanvasOverlay.tsx`'s `startResize` measures the layer, its parent's inside and, for an absolutely placed layer,
its drawn insets and what it snaps to, or the frame's box, and writes what comes back. `canvas/gesture.ts`'s
`followPress` follows the pointer in one gesture, holds the cursor, and on Escape reverts the document to a checkpoint
taken when the drag began, with the `ProjectDoc`'s `checkpoint` and `revert` from
`packages/multiplayer/src/project-doc.ts` (see "Cursors and Escape during a gesture").

### Padding, gaps and several layers on the canvas (PAR-169)

A selected layout's padding and gaps are handles, as in Figma: a short bar in the middle of each side's padding and of
each gap between its children, which hatches the space it changes while it's in use. Resize handles also take several
layers at once, resize from the middle with Alt, and hug or fill on a double-click.

- **Where the bars are.** Each side has one, even at padding 0, so padding can be dragged out of nothing. A side's press
  target runs from 4px inside the layout's edge, clear of the resize strip there, to the padding's inside, at least 8px
  deep and 24px along. A gap has one between each two children drawn in a single line, in a flex layout that doesn't
  wrap, at least 8px across; a grid or a wrap has gaps in two directions and no gap bars yet. A side or a gap shorter
  than 24px has none. Inside an instance, a layout's padding and gaps are the component's, so they have no bars.
- **A click on a child still selects it.** No press target covers a child, those placed absolutely included: each is cut
  back to the free space, and a side or a gap with less than 4px of it free has no bar. So padding of 0 drags out only
  where no child sits against that edge. Before, a target reached 8px in over the children, and clicks meant for them,
  such as on Titles' first line with no padding or on Header actions' empty row at its end, opened the box to type in,
  which then took the keys; the end-to-end tests caught it on #266.
- **Dragging.** Hovering or pressing a bar hatches its space and shows its value beside it, as pixels and a token: the
  length token it's bound to, or else its step of the spacing scale (`20 spacing-5`). Padding grows as its bar goes
  outwards, away from the content, on every side; a gap grows as its bar goes right in a row or down in a column. The
  value goes in whole steps from what's drawn, never below 0, and nothing changes until the pointer has gone 4px towards
  or away from the space. On the Dashboard's Content, padding `[8, 8]`, the left bar dragged 16px left makes
  `[8, 8, 8, 12]`. It writes as the pointer moves, as one undo step (Change padding or Change gap), and Escape takes it
  back, as a resize does (`gestures.resize`).
- **Alt and Alt+Shift.** Alt gives the opposite side the dragged side's value, and Alt+Shift every side, both read at
  each move, so letting go mid-drag puts the other sides back. Every side that changes is hatched. A layout has one gap,
  so a gap's bar changes them all, and while one is hovered or dragged every gap is hatched.
- **Tokens stay bound.** A side or a gap bound to a length token stays bound while the drag lands on a length token's
  value, its own first; between tokens it's steps. A number stays a number, even on a token's value.
- **Typing.** A click on a bar, or Enter on a focused one, opens a box beside it with the value, or the token's name
  when it's bound, selected. It reads what the inspector's length fields read (`20`, `1.5rem`, `+8`, a token's name),
  shows `px` after a plain number, which switches to rem (16 to the rem, so 16 becomes 1), and has the inspector's list
  of the project's length tokens and the spacing scale beside it, each with a bar drawn as the token previews draw
  spacing, in that unit. Enter or leaving it makes the change; Escape closes it; something it can't read stays with the
  reason under it, as the fields' do. The sides it changes are those held at the click.
- **Colors and hatching (PAR-797).** Padding and gaps are modes' green, as the Design panel's box model draws padding;
  margin is pink (`--canvas-margin`), which the canvas doesn't draw yet. Nothing is hatched while a layout is only
  selected. A bar hatches the space it changes while it's hovered, focused, typed in or dragged, as Figma does: 1px
  lines rising to the right, 8px apart along an edge, over a faint tint, the same at every zoom. A padding side is
  hatched along its whole edge, corners included, and the sides Alt or Alt+Shift change are hatched as one shape, so a
  corner is hatched once. A value's chip is the bar's color with near-black text, 7.9:1 on it.
- **The keyboard and assistive technology.** Each bar is a slider named after its side (Top padding, Gap 1), with its
  value and token as its text. Tab reaches it; Up or Right steps it one step, Down or Left back, Shift ten, Alt and
  Alt+Shift as for a drag; each press is its own undo step. The canvas's own arrow keys don't nudge meanwhile.
- **The hints and the keymap.** A bar's hint says "Drag, or click to type", and a padding bar's lists Alt for both sides
  and Alt+Shift for all sides, as `Kbd`. A layer's resize hint lists Alt for from the middle and says double-click to
  hug, Alt+double-click to fill. These keys are the keymap's gestures, which Keyboard shortcuts lists under Tools, and
  the handles read the same entries, so what's listed is what works.
- **A bar keeps the pointer while its hint opens (PAR-801).** A bar's hint lets the pointer through it, so the bar stays
  hovered, with its hatching and chip, until the pointer leaves the bar. The hint then closes, even when the pointer
  leaves onto it. Before, the hint's arrow slid in over a still pointer on a bar 12px thick, such as Gap 1 on the
  Dashboard's Content at 50%. The bar lost the hover, and its hatching and chip went until the pointer moved.
- **Several layers.** Two or more selected layers have one set of resize handles, on the box around them all. Each layer
  takes its share of the movement, its size across that box's, so they grow in proportion and the box's edge follows the
  pointer; each keeps where its layout puts it, and they don't snap. All of them start once the pointer has gone 4px.
  Two of the Dashboard's stat cards, 228px each, dragged 40px narrower from their right edge, are 52 steps wide each.
  One undo step (Resize layers). A selection holding a layer inside an instance has no handles.
- **From the middle.** Alt while resizing moves the opposite edge as far, so a layer in a layout grows by twice the
  pointer's movement and doesn't fill; an absolutely placed layer's inset moves back by half of what it grows, both
  insets of a layer stretched between them. It doesn't snap.
- **Hug and fill.** A double-click on a layer's handle makes its size on the handle's axes hug, Alt+double-click fill,
  for every layer the handle is on, one undo step (Set to hug or Set to fill). Along the layout's direction it takes
  `grow` away.

Code: the rules are in `@parity-app/editor`. `packages/editor/src/spacing-handles.ts`: `spacingHandles` says where the
bars go from a layout's measured boxes, `spacingDrag` follows a drag, `spacingStep` a key, `typedSpacing` and
`pickedSpacing` a typed or picked value, `changedSides` the sides held, and `spacingScaleName` and `spacingName` what a
label and a slider say, the steps of the scale being those the styling framework derives (`spacingSteps` in the app's
`tokens-store.ts`). `packages/editor/src/move-resize.ts`: `resizeGesture` and `resizeInsets` take `centre`,
`layersResize` follows several layers, and `layerSizeReset` hugs or fills. In the app, `canvas/SpacingHandles.tsx` draws
the bars, their hatching (`Hatching`, one shape per color), labels and sliders and the box a value is typed in, with
`sidesHeld` reading the keys, and each bar's hint through `chrome/Hint.tsx` with `passThrough`, which takes the hint out
of hit testing (Base UI's `disableHoverablePopup`); `canvas/spacing-colors.ts` is the one place the colors and hatching
are defined (`spacingColors` for padding, gaps and margin, `spacingChip` pairing a value's chip through `chipFor`,
`spacingHatch`); `canvas/spacing-edit.ts` measures a layout (`measureSpacing`, through `frameGeometry` and
`spacingMeasure` in `canvas/layer-measure.ts`, PAR-967), lists its length tokens (`lengthTokens`) and writes each edit
in the state the frame shows, a drag through `followPress`; `canvas/CanvasOverlay.tsx` shows them for a single selected
layout, puts handles around several layers (`resizeLayers`) and passes `centre` and fill. The keys are `gestures` in
`chrome/keymap.ts`, read through `holds` in `chrome/keys.ts`, and shown by `canvas/KeyHints.tsx`.

cleared it and closed the hint; the left bar was hatched while hovered and cleared after; focus on Gap 1 hatched it and
opened its hint, and Tab moved it to Gap 2. A run of key presses isn't one undo step, as the inspector's are (PAR-441).
Gap bars in a grid or a wrap, with column and row gaps, aren't done. A token whose length can't be worked out on
Parity's page, one built on a variable other than `--spacing`, isn't listed and can't be stayed on.

### Empty layouts (PAR-193)

A layout with nothing in it, which would draw nothing, takes at least 24px of the design along each axis its content
would size, outlined in dashes, so it can be seen, selected with a click and dropped into. This is on the canvas only.

- **A length the design gives it stays.** Along an axis with a fixed width or height, or a least size, it keeps what the
  design says, so an empty layout used as an 8px spacer is still 8px across; only the other axis gets the 24px. On an
  instance whose component's root is an empty layout, the instance's own width or height counts too. Filling and growing
  aren't lengths: in a grid, or with no space to share, they leave an empty layout at nothing, so it gets the 24px, and
  where they give it more, it keeps that. In a row, an empty column that's stretched keeps its stretched height.
- **It's empty when nothing is drawn in it** in the state and viewport shown, so a layout whose children the state hides
  counts too. The size and the dashes go once something is put in it; while a drag shows a copy of a layer in it, they
  stay.
- **Nothing drawn offscreen for anything but the canvas gets them** (PAR-888). Agents' screenshots and `Measure`,
  `problems`, exports, copying as a PNG and component previews draw an empty layout as the code does, so it takes no
  room it wouldn't take in the app and pushes nothing around. A frame's bitmap stands in for it on the canvas, so it
  keeps them, and a frame looks and measures the same asleep as awake.

Code: core's `emptyLayoutAttribute` in `packages/core/src/render.ts` marks an empty layout's element with the axes its
content would size (`data-canvas-empty-layout="width height"`), and the frame's root sheet in
`apps/desktop/src/renderer/frame.ts` gives it its least size (`emptyLayoutSize`) and dashes. The least size is
`!important`, to beat the `min-width: 0` a layout that fills is drawn with. A render job (`renderJob` in
`apps/desktop/src/shared/render-job.ts`) takes the attribute out of its tree with core's `withoutEmptyLayoutMarks`
unless it's marked `canvas`, which only the canvas's bitmaps (`frame-bitmaps.ts`) are. The sheet finds empty layouts by
that attribute, not by `:empty`: with `:empty` in it, a sheet every frame shares, closing a project with the pointer in
the window kept its frames in memory, about 1,800 DOM nodes each time on the example. `reopening.e2e.ts` caught it when
the tests before it left the pointer on the canvas.

Tests: `packages/core/src/render.test.ts`: which axes are marked for a layout that hugs, a fixed width, a least height,
growing in a row, and filling with a fixed height; a layout with layers unmarked; and one whose only layer the state
hides marked; `withoutEmptyLayoutMarks` taking the mark out of elements and slots, keeping other attributes and leaving
the tree given alone. `apps/desktop/src/shared/render-job.test.ts`: a job leaves the mark out unless it's for the
canvas. End to end (PAR-202), `apps/desktop/e2e/moving.e2e.ts` (2), with an empty row added after New project: it's 24px
wide and at least 24px high and is selected by a click, and a stat card dropped 6px inside its left edge at 50% goes
into it. Both failed before PAR-193: the row was 0px wide.

Gaps: the size label and the inspector show the 24px the canvas gives it, not the 0 the app would draw.
`reopening.e2e.ts` sees a leak like the one above only when the pointer is in the window, which depends on the tests run
before it; moving the pointer in after each close would make it certain.

### Cursors and Escape during a gesture (PAR-193)

While layers are dragged, a design is dragged by its title or a handle resizes, the cursor shows what's happening
wherever the pointer goes: grabbing for a drag, the handle's arrows for a resize. With the text tool, the canvas shows
the text cursor. Escape cancels each of these drags.

- **One lifecycle for every drag** (PAR-568). A resize, layers dragged in a layout, an absolutely placed layer dragged,
  designs dragged by a title and a box drawn on a frame's background all follow a press the same way. It becomes a drag
  once the pointer has gone 4 screen pixels, and only then begins its undo step, takes its checkpoint and holds its
  cursor, so a click begins none of them. The release keeps what the drag did. Escape, the pointer being cancelled and
  the window losing focus each do what the gesture's policy says:

  | Gesture                       | Escape                  | Pointer cancelled or window loses focus |
  | ----------------------------- | ----------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
  | Resize                        | takes it all back       | keeps it                                |
  | Layers dragged in a layout    | calls it off            | calls it off                            |
  | An absolutely placed layer    | takes it back           | takes it back                           |
  | Designs dragged by a title    | puts them back          | saves them where they are               |
  | A box on a frame's background | puts the selection back | puts the selection back                 |

  Taking back reverts the design to the checkpoint from when the drag began, leaving nothing to undo. A drag that's
  called off has written nothing, since it writes only when it's kept, and puts back what it showed: the drop preview,
  the designs on the canvas, the selection. Before PAR-568, a title drag and a box ended through listeners of their own
  and didn't hear the window losing focus (PAR-583). A title drag cut short that way never ended: the design stayed
  where it was dragged, unsaved, and the grabbing cursor covered the whole window even after the next click, since the
  title had lost the pointer and its listeners heard nothing more. A box went on selecting as the pointer moved with no
  button pressed, until the next click kept what it touched last.

- **Why it needed a layer of its own.** The cursor used to be set on the page's body, which showed only where nothing
  else set one: over the canvas tldraw sets its own cursor on everything it draws, and a title sets `default`. Now a
  transparent layer over the whole window holds the cursor for as long as the gesture lasts. The gestures follow the
  pointer through window listeners and find what's under it by layout boxes, so the layer takes nothing from them, and
  nothing under it reacts to hovering meanwhile.
- **The text tool** gives tldraw's canvas the browser's text cursor, by a rule more specific than tldraw's own, which
  takes the cursor of tldraw's tool, always Select or Hand here.
- **Escape on a design dragged by its title** puts every dragged design back where it was, saves nothing and adds no
  undo step, and leaves the design selected. The boards fly back there (see "How dragged things move").

Code: `apps/desktop/src/renderer/canvas/gesture.ts`: `followPress` follows a press, `gestures` holds each gesture's
policy, `dragThreshold` (from `@parity-app/editor`'s `move-resize.ts`) is the 4 pixels, `holdCursor` the layer, and
`onGestureEnd` hears how a gesture ends, as the right-click menu does too. The gestures are `canvas/CanvasOverlay.tsx`
(`startResize`), `canvas/layer-drag.ts` (`pressLayers` and `followAbsolute`), `canvas/ContainerUtil.tsx` (`dragByTitle`,
which gives the title the cursor too, since it has the pointer captured) and `canvas/select-box.ts` (`pressBackground`).
The text tool's rule is in `apps/desktop/src/renderer/styles.css`.

Tests:

- `canvas/gesture.test.ts`, without Electron, driving `followPress` with a plain `EventTarget` for the window and a
  session from `openTestSession` in `renderer/doc-fixtures.ts`: a press released short of 4 pixels is a click, with no
  undo step begun and no cursor held; the undo step, checkpoint and cursor begin once, as the press becomes a drag, and
  at the release the cursor goes, the step ends and nothing is left listening; Escape before the drag only ends it; a
  drag takes back what it wrote mid-drag and goes on in the same step; and Escape after a drag that wrote nothing leaves
  the file alone. For each of the five gestures, writing as the app's does (as the pointer moves, or once when kept):
  Escape leaves nothing to undo and the file clean; the window losing focus ends it as the table says, what it keeps
  being one undo step; and the release keeps it as one step. Also `onGestureEnd` (4): a gesture ending once, at the
  release, a cancelled pointer, the window losing focus or Escape, with nothing left listening after; Escape kept from
  going further, other keys let by; giving up without ending; and one gesture's end left to it when another follows.
- `canvas/CanvasOverlay.test.ts`, in Chrome, with the real mouse and the box's own code (`pressBackground`): a box from
  a frame's background puts the selection back when the window loses focus mid-box, and the pointer moving on over the
  cards and letting go selects nothing more (PAR-583). Against the box's listeners from before PAR-568 it fails, and the
  listeners left behind spoil the hover test after it.
- End to end (PAR-202), `apps/desktop/e2e/moving.e2e.ts` (5), reading the cursor of the element the browser finds under
  the pointer: grabbing while a stat card is dragged; grabbing while Dashboard is dragged by its title, on the title and
  200px off it; the arrows 80px below New project's right handle mid-resize, and not after; the text cursor over the
  stat cards with the text tool; and Dashboard's title dragged 160px, then Escape, leaving its board and its position as
  they were with nothing to undo. Each failed before PAR-193.

Gaps: what the system draws can't be read through the DevTools protocol, so the tests read the cursor the page asks for
at the pointer. Whether Chrome takes a captured title's cursor or the layer's doesn't matter, since both are grabbing.
The window losing focus is tested on the lifecycle, and for a box in Chrome with the window's `blur` sent by script, but
not end to end: Playwright tells the page it drives that it has the focus whatever the window does, so a real focus loss
never reaches it. A title drag's own part, saving the designs where they are, is checked only in the app. Checked in the
app on 2026-11-05 (PAR-583), on a copy of the example project, with the pointer sent over the DevTools protocol,
Playwright's focus emulation turned off, and the window minimized through Win32 mid-drag, which blurred the page. Before
PAR-568, Sign in dragged by its title and a box from its background both went on, as above. On main, the title drag
saved Sign in where it was as one undo step (Move screen) and let the cursor go, the box put the selection back, and
neither followed the pointer when it came back with no button pressed. The focus loss also took the title's pointer
capture (`lostpointercapture`) and sent no `pointercancel`, for a press sent over the protocol; a press of the system's
own mouse wasn't tried. That's why the old title drag, listening on the title, heard nothing more; `followPress` listens
on the window. Also checked on 2026-11-05 in Storybook's app window, with the pointer, Escape and the window's blur sent
by script: each of the five drags ended by Escape, by blur and by a release, as the table says, and a title drag with
the real pointer. Dragging a board by its background is tldraw's, with tldraw's own cursor, and Escape there is tldraw's
too.

### Snapping a dragged design (PAR-33)

A design dragged on the canvas locks to the designs and notes around it: along each axis, the nearest of its left,
centre and right (or top, middle and bottom) to any of theirs, within 8 screen pixels at the current zoom. Of lines just
as near, the first design's wins. A line shows where it locks, spanning both. Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) moves freely, and so
does turning snapping off under View; designs dragged together don't snap to each other.

Code: `snapBox` in `packages/editor/src/snap.ts` takes the boxes and the zoom and returns where the design goes and the
guides to draw, and `snaps` says whether a drag snaps, from the preference and Ctrl, for designs and layers alike;
`apps/desktop/src/renderer/canvas/snap.ts` (`snapPosition`) reads the shapes' boxes from tldraw and draws the guides as
tldraw's snap indicators, and `canvas/ContainerUtil.tsx` calls it while a design is dragged.

Tests: `packages/editor/src/snap.test.ts` (9): a left locking within 8 pixels and not past them, the distance counted on
screen at half and double zoom, centres and ends lining up, each axis on its own, the nearest line though a farther one
comes first, the first design's of lines just as near, the guides, and nothing around. Ctrl is tested with layers'
snapping, below.

Gaps: the pointer handling and the preference aren't tested; `apps/desktop/e2e/selecting.e2e.ts` drags a design with
snapping on, but doesn't check where it locks.

### Snapping layers while moving and resizing (PAR-174)

An absolutely placed layer dragged inside its design locks to its siblings and its parent, the way a dragged design
locks to the designs around it, with the same 8 screen pixels, the same red guides, and Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) or View's
snapping preference to move freely.

- **Edges and centres.** Along each axis, the nearest of its left, centre and right (or top, middle and bottom) to any
  of its siblings' or its parent's, within 8 screen pixels at the current zoom. Of lines just as near, a sibling's wins
  over the parent's, and the first sibling's over the next. The parent is the box its insets count from, inside its
  border: its containing block. That's the parent layout itself, since layouts are always positioned; only in a
  component's slot can it be another, the component's own box when it transforms or contains its content, or a box
  further up when nothing in the component is positioned. Either way a side snapped to that box's edge has an inset of
  0, and the distances shown are the insets written.
- **Even spacing.** Along each axis, it also takes the place that spaces it evenly with the siblings beside it across
  that axis, as in a row or a column: in the middle between two, or the same gap after or before a run of them that's
  already evenly spaced, so three or more are evenly spaced. Of an edge and an even space, the nearer wins; when both
  come to the same place, both show.
- **What shows.** A red guide along each line it locked to, spanning it and what it locked to; spacing marks in every
  gap of the evenly spaced run; and the distances to what it lined up with, drawn as Alt's redlines are, with the
  spacing step they come to: the gap to a sibling, or its four insets in its parent. They go when the drag ends, whether
  it's released, called off with Escape, or cut short by the pointer being cancelled or the window losing focus, and
  while Ctrl is held. Nothing is left listening after a gesture ends.
- **Exact where it locks.** Along an axis it locked along, it goes exactly there, to the half pixel, in fractions of a
  step where the line isn't on the scale; along an axis that didn't lock it moves in half steps as before.
- **Resizing.** Only the edges a handle drags lock, to the same lines; even spacing doesn't count, and the size goes to
  the half pixel rather than to whole steps. Shift on a corner keeps the proportions instead of snapping. Layers in a
  layout keep sizing in whole steps or filling, and don't snap.

On the Calendar's day, the Review slot sits 8 steps below the Planning slot and 8 above Lunch: dragged 6px down at 100%,
it stays, with marks in its gaps and Lunch's gap to the Usability slot, a guide down their left edges and 32px,
spacing-8 to Planning. Dragged 36px down, its bottom locks to Lunch's top at top 48, where it would be 49 with Ctrl.

Code: `snapLayer` in `packages/editor/src/snap.ts` (`@parity-app/editor`) takes the layer's box, its siblings' and its
parent's, the zoom and, for a resize, the edges the handle drags (`resizeEdges`, `resizedBox`), and returns where it
goes, the axes it locked, the guides, the distances (`distancesBetween`, which Alt's redlines use too) and the spacing
marks; `lockedEdgeMoves` says how far a resize's locked edges moved. `packages/editor/src/move-resize.ts` snaps with
them: `absoluteDrag` moves the layer exactly where it locked, and `layerResize` passes a resize's locked edges to
`resizeGesture`, which `resizeInsets` takes exactly; both give back where it locked.
`apps/desktop/src/renderer/canvas/layer-snap.ts` (`LayerSnapping`) measures the boxes in the frame when the gesture
begins (`snapScene` in `canvas/layer-measure.ts`, from `frameGeometry`, PAR-967), the parent's as the layer's
`offsetParent`, which is its containing block, and shows where the layer locked, the guides and marks as tldraw's snap
indicators, keeping the distances for `canvas/CanvasOverlay.tsx` to draw; the gesture clears them when it ends.
`canvas/layer-drag.ts` (`followAbsolute`) and `CanvasOverlay.tsx`'s `startResize` pass it in and show what comes back.
Both gestures end through `canvas/gesture.ts` (`followPress`), which tells them whichever way they end.

Tests:

  gap between them; a centre locking to the parent's, with the four insets; the distance counted on screen at half and

  handle doesn't drag left alone; the edges each handle drags; the same gap after a run and before one, in the middle

### Duplicating a design (CAN-47)

Duplicate (Ctrl+D) on a selected design puts the copy to the right of the original, top-aligned with it, at the first
place along that row where it keeps 160px clear of every design and note on the canvas, so it never covers the next
design and their titles don't meet. Several selected designs move as one block, and pasting designs into the project
they were copied from places them the same way.

- **A copy that lands off screen comes into view** (PAR-204). After Ctrl+D, Duplicate in the Layers menu, or a paste of
  designs, the canvas pans, at the zoom it's at, so the selected copy is seen 64px clear of the canvas's edges, room for
  its title. It moves the least it can along each axis, so what was in view stays as near as it can. A copy wider or
  taller than the view only needs its start in view, where its title is; otherwise its start comes to the view's start.
  A copy already in view leaves the view where it was. The pan takes 250ms.
- **At the size it's drawn at.** A copy beside its original is the original's size. A design pasted from another
  project, or whose original is no longer on the canvas, goes in the middle of the view, and its size is only known once
  its board draws it, so it's brought into view then, from its board's real size rather than a guess. One that isn't
  drawn within 2 seconds, as in a project that isn't showing, leaves the view alone.

Code: `freeSpotBeside`, `pastedPlacement` and `panToShow` in `packages/editor/src/placement.ts` (`@parity-app/editor`),
with `takenBounds`, `bringIntoView` and `bringIntoViewOnceSized` in `apps/desktop/src/renderer/canvas/free-space.ts`,
which read the canvas's shapes and move its camera, used by `chrome/designs.ts` (`duplicateDesign`) and
`canvas/clipboard.ts` (`pasteDesigns`). A board says when it has its size (`setBoardSized`, from
`canvas/ContainerUtil.tsx`'s resize observer).

right, a run of designs and gaps too narrow for the copy, a gap wide enough, designs well above or below the row, and
one just inside the gap below it; pasted copies (`pastedPlacement`) beside originals on the canvas at their size, and
copies from another project, or with an original gone, in the middle of the view with no size guessed; and bringing a
copy into view (`panToShow`): none needed when it's in view, right just far enough, left, up and down, a copy wider than
the view brought to its start, a taller one left alone while its top shows, and no margin unless asked. End to end

right, with no design or note within 160px, and Undo takes it away; Ctrl+D on Dashboard at 50%, whose copy starts off
screen, pans to it at the same zoom; Ctrl+C and Ctrl+V of it do the same; and Ctrl+D on Forgot password at 5%, whose
copy lands in view, leaves the view where it was.

Gaps: bringing a design pasted from another project into view once its board is sized has no automated test; it was
checked by reading. A copy pasted over the selection (Ctrl+Shift+V) or at the pointer doesn't pan, since it goes where
the person is looking.

### Arranging layers and designs (PAR-7)

Delete, Duplicate (Ctrl+D), Select all (Ctrl+A), Wrap in layout, Unwrap, the four orders, Hide, Align and Distribute act
on the whole selection as one undo step, labelled with how many things they touched.

- **They act on the outermost selected layers.** A layer inside another selected one moves with it, and selecting the
  design's root leaves nothing to arrange.
- **Delete selects the layout that held the last deleted layer,** or the design when that was its root.
- **Duplicate puts each copy just after its original,** in its layout or slot, with fresh ids for it and everything in
  it, and selects the copies.
- **Select all picks the selected layer's siblings** in its layout or slot, or every design when no layer is selected.
- **Wrap in layout lays the new layout out as the parent lays out the layers** as the frame shows it: in the state being
  edited, with the variant options the board shows and the frame's viewport (PAR-464). A row in a row, with the parent's
  gap. Layers in different layouts can't be wrapped together, and a message says so.
- **Unwrap leaves a layout's layers where it was** and selects them; on anything but a layout it says to select one.
- **Ordering moves a layer among its siblings.** Later paints in front, as in CSS, so Bring forward moves it later in
  its layout and down the Layers list. An order that wouldn't move it records nothing.
- **Align on layers works in their layouts,** as the frame shows them: in the state being edited, with the variant
  options the board shows and the frame's viewport (PAR-464). A layer aligns by itself on its layout's cross axis
  (`alignSelf`), and along the main axis the layout moves all its children (`justifyContent`). So in a layout a variant
  turns into a row, Align right sets `justifyContent: "end"` on the layout, in that variant, rather than `alignSelf` on
  the layer. Layers in a component's slot stay as they are.
- **Align on designs lines them up on the canvas** by their edges or centers, within the span of them all, and needs
  two. **Distribute spaces three or more evenly** between the outermost two, across or down. Positions are rounded to
  whole pixels, and a move that changes nothing records nothing.

Code: the rules are in `packages/editor/src/arrange.ts` (`@parity-app/editor`).
`apps/desktop/src/renderer/chrome/arrange.ts` applies them to the selection and the document, measures designs' boxes on
the canvas and shows the messages. Hide is core's `toggleHidden`.

Tests: `packages/editor/src/arrange.test.ts`: the outermost layers and the root; deleting and what's selected next (in a
layout, the root and a slot); duplicating in place with fresh ids (in a layout, a slot, a copied layout's children, and
nothing to copy); siblings in a layout and a slot; wrapping in a row, a column and another state, with the shared
fixture's card in its Inline option and in a viewport, and layers that can't be wrapped; unwrapping, and layers that
aren't layouts; each order in a layout and a slot, and orders that wouldn't move; aligning on the cross and main axes in
two states, in a row a variant makes and a column a viewport shows, and in a slot; aligning designs by edges and
centers, with a box offset from its position; distributing across and down whatever the selection's order; and moving
designs in whole pixels.

Gaps: the commands, menus and messages have no automated test. They didn't change when the rules moved into the package.

### Locking layers and designs (PAR-192)

Ctrl+Shift+L locks the selected layers, or the selected designs, and unlocks them once they're all locked, as one undo
step ("Lock layer", "Unlock screen"). Lock is also in the Object menu ("Lock or unlock"), the canvas menu under Hide,
and a Layers row's menu beside Hide, each reading Unlock when everything selected is locked.

- **A locked layer can't be selected or moved on the canvas,** nor can anything inside it. A click, a double-click or
  hovering goes to the layer around it, as if it weren't there, and a box drawn from the frame's background doesn't
  touch it.
- **A locked design is left to the canvas,** as tldraw leaves a locked shape: a click on it selects nothing, a press
  draws tldraw's box over it, its title doesn't drag it, nothing is dropped into it, and it gets the empty canvas's
  menu. Its layers are locked with it.
- **Layers still selects them.** Selected there, a locked layer or design is outlined on the canvas without resize or
  spacing handles, and changes from the inspector and the keys, nudging included; only the canvas's pointer leaves it
  alone.
- **Each row has a lock,** left of the eye, that locks or unlocks the layer or design without selecting it. It shows
  while the row is hovered and stays on a locked one. A layer locked by a layer or design around it shows a faded lock
  while hovered, which isn't a button, and its tooltip says what locks it ("Locked with Features"). The page has none,
  since locking it is locking the design, and neither do layers inside an instance, which are the component's. Like the
  eye, the lock isn't in the tab order.
- **It's saved in the .par** as `locked: true` on the layer or the design, the same in every state and screen size;
  unlocking takes it away.

Code: the rules are in `packages/editor/src/locking.ts` (`lockSource`, `unlockedPath`, `toggleLockedLayers`,
`setDesignLocked`), and `locked` is in core's schema (`document.ts`). The canvas leaves locked layers out of what's
under the pointer in `canvas/hit.ts` (`underPoint`), out of a box in `canvas/select-box.ts`, and handles off them in
`CanvasOverlay.tsx`; a locked design's board is a locked tldraw shape (`CanvasEditor.tsx`), and its title doesn't drag
it (`ContainerUtil.tsx`). The command is `toggleLockedSelection` in `chrome/arrange.ts`, the row's lock is in
`chrome/LayerTree.tsx`, and the menus are `canvas-menu.ts` and `layers-menu.ts`.

Tests:

- `packages/editor/src/locking.test.ts` (9): locking and unlocking, all locked when only some were, the root, a layer
  inside an instance and a missing layer left alone, the lock kept through parsing a project; what locks a layer
  (itself, a layer around it, its design, its instance); what's under the pointer cut at a locked layer, the design's
  lock left to the canvas; and Unlock read only when every design is locked.
- `chrome/canvas-menu.test.ts` and `chrome/layers-menu.test.ts`: Lock in each menu, unavailable inside an instance and
  on the root, and in a design's menu.
- `chrome/LayerTree.stories.tsx`: LockedFromItsLock (a row's lock, and a layer inside reading "Locked with Hero") and
  LockedDesign (the design's lock, its layers, and Unlock in its menu). Their play functions passed in Storybook on
  2026-11-16.
- `e2e/menus.e2e.ts`: the canvas menu lists Lock with Ctrl+Shift+L.

Gaps: clicking through a locked layer, a locked design ignoring clicks and its title, and Ctrl+Shift+L were tried on the

### Inserting, Make component and new designs (PAR-32)

Components, component designs and images go in from the Assets panel and Quick insert; Make component turns layers into
a component design; the Layers panel's add buttons start new designs. Each is one undo step, and selects what it made.

- **A drop lands in the slot under the pointer** (PAR-205), in the deepest of the design's own layouts there, or of its
  components' slots that hold layers (PAR-419), as a dropped image file, Paste here and the text tool land
  (`placeAtPoint`, through `measureHere`, `slotHere` and `slotAt`, PAR-570): in a grid or a wrapping row the line of
  children the pointer is on comes first, then the slot along it, so a card dropped on the second row of Projects' grid
  goes there, not in the first row. In a layout that's absolutely placed as the board shows it, it goes last, placed at
  the pointer in half steps of the spacing scale. While dragging, the layout is outlined and a line shows the slot, or a
  corner marks the pointer where it goes in an absolutely placed layout. A drop on the empty canvas makes a screen there
  (PAR-546, below); one over a design where there's no layout says so.
- **A click inserts at the selection:** into a selected layout, at its end; just after any other selected layer, in its
  layout or slot; or at the end of a selected design's root. With nothing selected it makes a frame in the middle of the
  view (PAR-546); with a design selected that has nowhere for it, a message says to select a layout.
- **What goes in is ready to show something.** A component gets its required props (an option's first value, `false`,
  `0` or its own name, unless they have a default) and its name as text when it takes children. A library's part comes
  inside the parents it needs that aren't around the layout already, with their samples.
- **A name goes in only where it fits (PAR-518).** A component whose own element sets its size gets no name, since
  "Avatar" in a 32px circle showed as "Avata": the props reader marks it `fixedSize` when the classes on the outermost
  element it returns give it a width (`size-8`, `w-10`), a height under a line (`h-px`) or `@container`, in a project's
  code or a library's compiled JavaScript. A library's part takes what its library's samples give it instead of its
  name: its own sample's children or text, or none when the sample gives none, as for a Separator, a Checkbox or
  AttachmentAction, an icon button. A part without a sample of its own takes the children the first of the library's
  other samples to use it gives it, so MarkerIcon and AttachmentMedia, whose icons Marker's and Attachment's samples
  can't show, hold nothing. A part no sample shows keeps its name. A component design goes in as a linked instance or,
  from a library's menu, a detached copy. An image is 80 spacing steps (320px) wide, its height following its shape.
- **The undo step says what was added:** "Add Button" (the component's name without its library), "Add component", "Add
  copy" or "Add image".
- **Make component** puts the component design at the end of the project file, 640px above the topmost design on the
  canvas, lined up with the design it came from, so components sit above screens. An instance replaces each occurrence,
  and the step is "Extract" and its name. It's refused, changing nothing, unless the design renders the same in every
  state, viewport and variant option, as its board shows each, with the defaults of the params the design binds
  (PAR-486). Every option of every variant is checked, not only the one the board shows (PAR-493), each with the other
  variants as the board shows them, and the message names the option: "Extracting would change how Team looks (Default,
  desktop, Compact), so it wasn't done". So a variant option that changes something inside the part, shown or not, or a
  param default a layer in it shows, refuses it rather than losing the change. A component design's Params section lists
  its instances, across every design.
- **A new design goes 240px to the right of everything on the canvas,** top-aligned with the topmost design. A screen
  starts as a padded page with its name as a heading, a component as a small padded layout on a 480px frame.

Code: the rules are in `packages/editor/src/insert.ts`, `components.ts`, `create.ts` and `placement.ts`
(`@parity-app/editor`), with the new layer's props and label in `componentNode` and a library part's parents and samples
in `withLibraryContext`, both in `packages/core/src/library-insert.ts`, and `fixedSize` read from the classes
`packages/code/src/props.ts` finds on a component's own element (`ownClasses`) by the styles provider's `setsOwnSize`.
The app's `canvas/insert.ts` finds where a drop lands through `placeAtPoint` in `canvas/paste-here.ts`, the step drops,
Paste here and the text tool share, and applies an insert to the selection and the document, `chrome/components.ts`
measures the designs and applies Make component, and `chrome/create.ts` adds a new design and zooms to it. Every design
added to or deleted from a file, by the editor or an agent, goes through core's `addDesigns` and `removeDesigns` in
`packages/core/src/designs.ts`, and a new file starts as its `emptyDocument`, so the format's version is written only in
`formatVersion` (PAR-1052).

### A new design's id (PAR-1108)

A new design's id is a stem made from its name and five random characters, `pricing-k3f9q` for Pricing: lowercased, each
run of other characters one hyphen, `design` when nothing is left, then `generateId`'s characters, as a layer's id has.
Two people who each add a design called Pricing get different ids, so a project document several people edit doesn't
collide when their changes meet (docs/proposals/multiplayer.md, Ids).

- **Every new design takes one:** New screen, New component and New frame, a frame from the frame tool, layers or an
  item with nothing to go into, dropped images, Make component, Duplicate, and an agent's `CreateDesign` and
  `ExtractComponent`.
- **A pasted design always gets a new id,** even when the one it was copied with is free, so two people pasting one copy
  don't make the same id. An instance among the pasted designs follows its component to the component's new id.
- **Ids already in files stay as they are.** A design keeps its id when it's renamed, and states, variant options, modes
  and viewports still take ids from their names alone (`uniqueId`), since they're only unique inside one design or
  project setting.

Code: `designId` in `packages/core/src/edit.ts` (`@parity-app/core`), with the stem from `idStem` in `modes.ts`; used by
`create.ts`, `new-screen.ts`, `frames.ts`, `components.ts`, `drop-files.ts` and `clipboard.ts` (`copyDesigns`) in
`packages/editor`, `chrome/designs.ts` (`duplicateDesign`) in the desktop app, and `packages/agent/src/workspace.ts`.

Tests: `packages/core/src/edit.test.ts` ("designId", 2): the stem and five characters, `design` for a name with no
letters or digits, and two designs with one name apart. `packages/editor/src/clipboard.test.ts` ("pasting designs", 4)
and `paste-over.test.ts`: a new id even when the copied one is free, two copies of one design apart, and an instance
following a copied component but not one outside the paste. The tests for each way of making a design check its id has
the name's stem and five characters.

### New screen, New component and the empty canvas (PAR-546)

Making a screen or component is one visible step, as PAR-541's approved designs show, without the start in the middle of
an empty canvas that PAR-560 dropped: New screen and New component are everywhere a command is, and whatever lands on
empty space on the canvas makes a frame there (PAR-545; see Frames, below).

- **New screen (Ctrl+Alt+N) and New component (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+N)** are in the keymap's Object group, so the Keyboard
  shortcuts dialog lists them and their keys work on the canvas, not in a text field. They lead File, above opening a
  project, and Object, above Insert…, each with its keys. Each makes an empty screen or component right of everything,
  selects it and zooms to it, as Layers' + always has.
- **Search actions finds them by the start of words.** Each typed word must start a word of an action's name or group,
  in any order, and a name that starts with everything typed comes first, so "new" lists New screen and New component
  and nothing with n, e and w scattered through it, and "fit zoom" still finds Zoom to fit.
- **The canvas's right-click menu around the designs** starts with New screen, New component and Insert…, each with its
  keys, then Paste here, then Select all and Zoom to fit. New screen and New component put the new one's top left where
  the canvas was right-clicked and select it, leaving the view where it is. With no screen, component or note on the
  canvas, Select all and Zoom to fit are unavailable. Over a design the menu is as it was. It's as wide as its longest
  item, so New component and its keys stay on one line.
- **Layers' + always shows** beside Screens and Frames, with its name and keys in the tooltip; Routes has none, as
  they're read from the app's code. Since PAR-187 the headings have no count. An empty group's row is a button that
  makes the first one: "No screens yet. New screen", the action in the kind's color. Enter or Space on either makes one,
  rather than renaming the selected row as Enter in the tree does.
- **The inspector with nothing selected** asks for "a screen, component or frame on the canvas or in Layers", whatever
  is on the canvas.
- **What lands on empty space on the canvas makes a frame there,** by one rule. Its top left is where it landed, it
  holds what landed in a padded column that hugs it, and it's selected, as one undo step named for what landed ("Paste
  layer", "Paste 7 layers", "Add Badge", "Add vertical layout"). It's named after what's in it, never "Pasted": one
  layer as Layers names it (a component without its library, "Button"; an instance after its design; text by its words;
  a layout Column or Row); several images Images; several other layers the first and how many more ("Nav and 6 more").
  - Layers pasted on the empty canvas with Paste here, or with nothing selected with Ctrl+V, in the middle of the view;
    and the insert picker's Text and layouts with nothing selected.
  - A component, component design or image from the Components panel dropped on the empty canvas, where a corner in the
    layer color marks its top left while dragging; or clicked in the panel or picked in the insert picker with nothing
    selected, in the middle of the view. It goes in as inserting it into a layout would: with its required props, a
    library part inside the parents it needs, and a detached copy as the layers its design shows.
  - Image files dropped on the empty canvas, named after the file or Images (see Dropping image files, below).
  - Over a design where there's no layout under the pointer, nothing lands, and a message says "There's no layout here
    to drop into", as it does for files. With a design selected that has nowhere to insert, the insert picker and the
    Components panel both say "Select a layout, or a layer to add it after".
  - Pasted text makes a text frame, as the text tool does (see Frames, below).

Code: the commands are `newScreen` and `newComponent` in `chrome/keymap.ts` and `chrome/actions.ts`, run through
`createDesign` in `chrome/create.ts`, which takes a point for the canvas menu. `AppMenu.tsx` (`NewItems`),
`canvas-menu.ts` (`canvasMenu`, around the designs) and `CanvasMenu.tsx` (`run`) show them; `matchWords` in
`packages/editor/src/find-anything.ts` is Search actions' matching (see Search actions, below); the headings and empty
rows are in `chrome/LayerTree.tsx`, and the inspector's prompt in `DesignPanel.tsx`. The rule and the names are
`packages/editor/src/new-screen.ts` (`layersName`, `designOfLayers`, `designOfItem`); the app's `canvas/new-screen.ts`
finds the empty canvas (`emptyCanvasAt`) and the middle of the view and adds a frame of layers, `canvas/insert.ts` adds
one of an item (`addFrameOfItem`, from `insertAtSelection` and drops), and `canvas/clipboard.ts` and
`canvas/CanvasDrop.tsx` call them.

### Frames and the frame tool (PAR-545)

Frames are the light kind of design, beside screens and components, as PAR-540's approved exploration showed them
(removed once built, PAR-798), on PAR-539's model: a frame is drawn once, at its own size, in the project's primary
mode, with one state, and isn't written to code.

- **On the canvas a frame has no board:** its name above it, smaller and quieter than a board's title, with lucide's
  Frame icon, neutral until it's selected and then in the layer color, and the design at its own size, filled with the
  primary mode's background. It has no state or mode menus, captions or gutter, and its outline is square. Its name runs
  past a narrow frame rather than being cut off. Selected, its size shows under it, and its handles on the right, the
  bottom and the corner resize it; a double-click on one goes back to the primary mode's width or the content's height.
- **The frame tool (F, or A as in Figma)** sits after Move and Hand, beside Text, in its own group. The pointer is a
  crosshair, over the designs too. A drag draws a frame, with its size under it as it grows, snapping each edge within 6
  screen pixels to the edges of the designs around it, with a guide where it snapped; Ctrl or Cmd draws freely, and
  Escape draws nothing. A click without a drag makes a 100 × 100 frame. Either is named Frame 1, Frame 2 and so on,
  selected, with the move tool back, as one undo step, "Draw frame".
- **The frame tool's menu,** the arrow beside it, lists each viewport the modes use once, with the modes that use it and
  its size, a viewport with only a width taking the height of the device nearest it. With a frame selected a size
  resizes it ("Resize frame to Mobile"); otherwise it adds a frame at that size in the middle of the view. New screen
  and New component sit below the sizes, with their keys.
- **Text on the empty canvas:** T and a click in empty space makes a text layer, "Text", in a frame that hugs it, with 2
  steps of padding, and edits it at once. The frame takes the text's name as it's edited in place, until it's renamed. T
  over a design still adds text where a drop would land. Notes already in a file still show; nothing makes a new one.
- **A frame that hugs its content** (its root layout's width is Hug) is as wide as its root is drawn: the canvas
  measures the root at its content's width, rounded up to a whole pixel, and keeps that as the frame's size, without an
  undo step of its own. A width of its own, from the handles, the menu's sizes or the inspector, stops it hugging.
- **Whatever lands on the empty canvas makes a frame,** as "New screen, New component and the empty canvas" above says,
  hugging what's in it and named after it. Pasted text makes a text frame, as the text tool does.
- **The inspector for a frame:** its name, with the kind's icon beside it; where it's drawn ("Drawn in Desktop Light",
  with the primary mode's crown) and that it isn't written to code; then its root layout's layout, spacing, size and
  fill straight away, with no states, modes or params. The size rows are the frame's own size: a fixed width or height
  resizes it, Hug makes it hug its content, and Fill or Auto puts back the primary mode's width or the content's height.
  Export is at the foot, as for any design.
- **Convert to,** in every design's title menu ("Convert to component", "Convert to screen", "Convert to frame", with
  each kind's icon), and as Make component's Convert to component in the canvas and Object menus. A frame becomes a
  screen or a component at once, keeping its size as its preview's, with a toast ("Converted to a component") whose Undo
  makes it a frame again. A screen or component becomes a frame at once when it drops nothing; otherwise a dialog lists
  what goes (states after the first, previews beside the main one, params, and each design's instances, which become
  plain layers), with Cancel and Convert to frame. Each is one undo step, and converting a component detaches its
  instances in the same step.
- **Layers lists Frames** after Routes and Screens once there are any; its + picks the frame tool.

Code: the rules are `packages/editor/src/frames.ts` (`drawnFrame`, `nextFrameName`, `snapToEdges`, `draggedBox`,
`framePresets`, `frameOfText`, `textFrameRenamed`, `hugsContent`, `fittedFrame`, `withFrameSize`, `frameRootShown` and
`frameRootStored`, `instanceCount` and `detachInstancesOf`), with `turnInto` in `kinds.ts`, `withFrame` and
`frameResize` in `move-resize.ts`, and the empty canvas's rule in `new-screen.ts` (`landedStyle`) and `drop-files.ts`.
In the app, `canvas/frame-tool.ts` draws and places frames, `canvas/ContainerView.tsx` draws a frame without a board
(`FrameView`) and keeps a hugging one fitted (`useFitToContent`), `canvas/CanvasOverlay.tsx` takes the frame tool's
press, draws the frame being dragged and the selected frame's size, `canvas/new-screen.ts` adds a text frame
(`addFrameOfText`), `chrome/FloatingToolbar/FrameMenu.tsx` has the tool's menu, `chrome/designs.ts` converts
(`setDesignKind`), `chrome/convert-to-frame.ts` says what a conversion drops and `chrome/ConvertToFrameDialog.tsx` asks,
and `chrome/style-editor.ts` maps a frame's root size to its own.

- End to end (PAR-202), `apps/desktop/e2e/frames.e2e.ts`: F and a drag draws Frame 1, selected, with the move tool back,

## Tools

What the floating controls on the canvas hold, and how a review tool takes over the toolbar.

### The toolbar, review tools and Zoom (PAR-780, PAR-795, PAR-893)

- **The toolbar floats at the bottom of the canvas,** in the middle, in three groups: what the pointer does; the colored
  tools that add things, Frame (F), Text (T) and the review button; then the commands that open a dialog or a search,
  Insert, Find references and Search actions, which stay plain. Move and select (V), Hand (H) and Interact (I) share one
  button, which shows the one picked last; the arrow beside it switches, and says Space and a drag pans with any tool.
  Frame's icon is in the layer blue and Text's in text's green, as everywhere they show (PAR-792). A picked tool is
  white on the selection blue. Frame's arrow holds its sizes, then New screen in screen blue and New component in
  component purple. The arrow keys move through the tools; the commands are Tab stops of their own.
- **The floating bars** sit on a surface a step off white on the light theme, and their groups are split by lines etched
  into them: a groove with a highlight on its right, through the bar's padding to its border. A picked tool's button, or
  a stamp's chip, boings (picking a review tool warps the bar instead), and a pressed control dips and springs back;
  with reduced motion they keep still.
- **The review button** shows the review tool picked last, Comment at first, in its color when it isn't picked: Comment
  is pink, and each kind of annotation has its own hue. Its arrow lists Comment, with C, then, under Annotate with
  Shift+T, each kind of annotation: Behaviour, Content, Accessibility and Development. C picks Comment, and Shift+T
  annotates in the kind picked last, Behaviour at first.
- **A review tool warps the toolbar into its bar.** A kind of annotation's bar has its options as stamps, the picked one
  showing its name, then Suggest and Done; Comment's says Commenting and what a click does, then Done. The canvas goes
  to Move and select, so a click selects rather than adding text.
- **Putting it down:** Done or Esc warps the toolbar back, onto the tool picked before. Esc first stops editing, as
  before, and only then puts the review tool down; with none picked it goes to Move and select, the parent, then
  nothing. Picking a tool by its key or button puts the review tool down and picks that tool. Picking another review
  tool while one is picked keeps the tool to go back to.
- **The warp.** The bar's width springs to the side that's showing. The leaving side's parts fly out, and the entering
  side's land in a ripple outward from the review button, with a flash and a ring in the review tool's color, or the
  layer blue going home. With reduced motion the sides cross-fade. Focus moves to the side showing, to its picked
  control or its first; the hidden side can't be reached by pointer, keyboard or screen reader. The toolbar is named for
  its side ("Toolbar", "Comments", "Behaviour annotations"). A focused button's ring shows whole at either end of the
  bar. The hidden side takes no room, so a bar that hasn't measured its sides yet fits the side showing (PAR-1192).
  Before, it took the hidden review bar's 400px around the tools' 315px whenever its ResizeObserver hadn't reported, as
  in a window the system hides, leaving empty space at both ends. Checked on 2026-11-16 in a dev copy whose window was
  covered: with the hidden side out of the flow, the bar measured 324px around the tools.
- **Zoom floats at the top right:** Zoom out, the level, Zoom in and Zoom to fit, each with its keys in its tooltip. The
  level is a button that goes to 100%, named "Zoom to 100%, now 64%". Each acts on the project's canvas. Undo and Redo
  left the canvas for the Edit menu and their keys. An extension's `topRight` layer, such as the live room's avatar
  stack, sits just left of Zoom on its row (PAR-1293).

Code: the review rules are `packages/editor/src/review.ts` (`startReview`, `pickReview`, `stopReview`, `reviewToolFor`
and `isReviewTool`). In the app, `renderer/selection.ts` keeps each project's review (`startReviewing`, `stopReviewing`,
`useReview`, and `setTool` putting it down); `chrome/keymap.ts` and `chrome/actions.ts` have Comment and Annotate, and
`stepBack` in `chrome/actions.ts` puts the review tool down on Esc. `chrome/FloatingToolbar/` has the toolbar:
`FloatingToolbar.tsx`, `Tools.tsx`, `MoveMenu.tsx`, `FrameMenu.tsx`, `ReviewButton.tsx` and `tool-details.ts`, with the

`chrome/toolbar-parts.tsx` has the parts the floating bars share, and `chrome/ZoomControls.tsx` is Zoom. Insert, Find

`collaboration/annotations/` has the review tools' bars: `annotation-kinds.ts` names and colors each review tool,
