### Auto width, auto height and fixed text (PAR-175)

A text layer sizes in one of Figma's three ways (for a text layer; a component's text sizes as the component does). The
mode is read from the layer's width and height, so it isn't a separate setting that could disagree with them, and the
resize handles change it as Figma's do. The inspector's Resizing control left the panel with PAR-923, since it has no
approved control yet; `textSizingEdit` still makes each switch, for the control that replaces it.

- **Auto width:** `width: { size: "hug" }`. The layer is as wide as its line and never wraps for its parent, only at a
  maximum width if it has one, as in Figma. It's drawn `width: max-content`, Tailwind's `w-max`; hug on other layers
  stays `fit-content`.
- **Auto height:** any other width, or none, and no height. It wraps at its width and grows down. A text layer with no
  width wraps at the one its layout gives it, so that's auto height too, which is what text added to a layout starts as.
- **Fixed:** a height as well, a length, a token or fill. It keeps that height whatever the text, and text past it
  overflows, as in Figma.
- **Switching keeps it where it's drawn.** Auto width sets hug and drops the height (and the older `grow`). Auto height
  turns a hugging width into the width it's drawn at, rounded up to whole spacing steps so the text doesn't wrap again,
  keeps any other width, and drops the height. Fixed does the same for the width and fixes the height it's drawn at,
  rounded up too, or keeps the one it has. In a column, where the older `grow` fills the height, both drop it too; in a
  row it fills the width, which they keep. Each is one undo step. Dragging a side handle of auto width text fixes its
  width, so it becomes auto height; dragging the bottom fixes its height, so it becomes fixed.
- **Several layers, states and variants.** With several text layers selected, each is measured in its own box, so each
  keeps its own size, and each one's own parent decides whether `grow` goes. In a selection of text and other layers,
  Resizing changes only the text. In a state, a variant or an instance, a height or `grow` the design sets would show
  again if the change only dropped it, so auto width and auto height set the height to hug, and `grow` to false, over
  it. Resetting Resizing there takes back all three of width, height and `grow`, so no `grow: false` stays behind
  (PAR-582).

Code: what the editor edits, what it selects, the modes and switching between them are
`packages/editor/src/text-editing.ts` (`editableText`, `textToEdit` and `withEditedText`, which read and write the text
in one state, `wordAt`, `openingSelection`, `textSizing`, `withTextSizing`, and `textSizingKeys`, the properties a
switch writes and a reset clears). Drawing hug text as `max-content` is `textCss` in `packages/core/src/render.ts`. The
editor is `apps/desktop/src/renderer/canvas/TextEditor.tsx`: it finds the character under the double-click from the
text's own ranges, measures the text when the canvas's overlays do (`canvas/overlay-scheduler.ts`), its content box and
its own scale through `frameGeometry` (`canvas/frame-geometry.ts`, PAR-967), and handles the keys. The double-click
passes its point through `SelectionStore.setEditing` (`selection.ts`), from `canvas/CanvasOverlay.tsx`. A switch's edit
is `textSizingEdit` in `packages/editor/src/style-editing.ts`, rounding each layer's measure up with `stepUp`. The
agent's skill says how text sizes in `packages/cli/skills/document.md`.

### Inline text, alignment and long words (PAR-898)

A text layer whose tag is drawn inline, `span`, `label` or `strong`, has no box of its own outside a flex or grid
layout, as in a component's slot or a table cell, so a width, height, minimum or maximum, `textAlign` or `lineClamp: 1`
would do nothing there. Given any of these, it's drawn `display: block`, so a `span` with a maximum width is cut off at
it and a number in a table cell lines up at its end. Without them it stays inline, in the line of text around it. More
than one line already draws its own box, which clamps it. A `p` or a heading is a block anyway.

`overflowWrap` says where a word too long for its line breaks, such as a web address in a narrow column: `anywhere`,
which also lets a table cell or a hugging layout narrow to fit, or `break-word`, which breaks it only once it can't fit
on a line of its own. Set on a layout, the text inside takes it. Unset, a long word runs out of its box. The Text
section has no control for it yet; agents set it.

Code: `text` (with `boxKeys`) and `type` in `packages/style-schema/src/declare.ts`, the `overflowWrap` key in
`packages/style-schema/src/model.ts`, and `inlineTags` in `packages/core/src/render.ts`, which tells the style a text's
tag is inline.

Tests: `packages/style-schema/src/declare.test.ts`, declarations: inline text given a maximum width and one line, or an
alignment, drawn as a block; several lines keeping the box that clamps them; inline text with nothing that needs a box
staying inline; and `overflowWrap`. `packages/core/src/render.test.ts`, sizing: in a component's slot, a `span` aligned
to the end drawn as a block, and a plain `strong` and a `p` with a maximum width left as they are.

Gaps: no warning says when a style has no effect for another reason. Checked in an isolated copy of the app on
2026-11-11, in a shadcn table: a `span` with `maxWidth: { step: 40 }` and `lineClamp: 1` in a cell was cut off with an
ellipsis at 160px, a `span` aligned to the end lined up at its cell's end, and a web address with
`overflowWrap: "anywhere"` wrapped onto three lines in a 224px column.

## Saving and undo

What goes through Save and Undo, and where an edit lands when the board shows a state or a variant.

### One history, saved together (PAR-164)

Every change people or agents make goes into one history per project, and stays unsaved until Save (Ctrl+S).

- **What's undoable:** every edit to a design or a text note, the modes, and token values. An agent's call is one step,
  its designs, modes and tokens together, and undoing it leaves edits made while it ran. What a board shows (the state,
  Show every state, the modes beside it, the variant picked in its title bar) isn't undoable, and Undo leaves it as it
  is, but it's saved in the `.par`, so changing it marks the file unsaved.
- **What Save writes:** each `.par` with changes, and the token values into the project's stylesheet (`src/index.css` in
  the example), together. A token edit shows in every frame at once, since the stylesheet every frame shares is edited
  in place, but nothing is written until Save. Don't save, when closing the project or quitting, leaves the stylesheet
  as it was. With Save automatically on, token values are written about 300ms after the edit, as files are.
- **A `.par` keeps its key order** (PAR-1288): each object is written with its keys in the order the file on disk has
  them, and a new key goes after the key it follows, so a save changes only the lines that changed, also in a file
  written by hand or by another tool (`projectFileText` in `packages/core/src/file-order.ts`, which `saveDocument` in
  `apps/desktop/src/utility/projects.ts` writes with). Tested in `packages/core/src/file-order.test.ts`
  ("projectFileText"): the file's order kept, a new key placed after the one it follows, a key taken out left out, an
  array's items matched by `id` wherever they moved, and the value's order kept when the file isn't JSON.
- **Undo after a save** puts the value back on the canvas, and the next Save writes the value the stylesheet had before.
  A value given to a theme that had none (a dark `--radius`), saved and then undone, is taken out of the stylesheet
  again by the next Save (PAR-420), from every block of that theme that declares it, and a block left empty goes with
  it, so a value Save added in a new `.dark` leaves the file as it was. Frames drawn offscreen stop drawing it once it's
  undone, without a reopen.
- **Clean again.** A file is clean whenever it's back to what was saved: by undoing, as before, and now also by changing
  it back. Turning Show every state on and off again, or showing another state and then the base one, leaves the file
  clean, also when the file wrote its view out in full (`"allStates": false`, the base state's id). A view is kept tidy:
  what it says by default (every state off, no modes beside, the base state) isn't written.
- **A failed write** to the stylesheet says where: the save notice and the status bar say which token and which file
  ("Couldn't write --primary to src/index.css: EPERM…"), the Tokens panel shows the same at its top with Try again, and
  the row of each token not written says "Not written to the stylesheet". The values stay on the canvas, unsaved. A
  stylesheet changed since its values were read fails the same way, writing nothing.
- **An agent's call lands over what's here now** (PAR-278): only the designs it changed, created or deleted are applied,
  so the person's edits to other designs, in the same file too, and another agent's call stay. Each design the call
  changes or deletes must still be as the call read it; one already as the call left it, changed the same way or deleted
  here too, counts as applied. A design the call created conflicts when one with its id was added here, and modes the
  call set conflict when they changed here since. Any conflict refuses the whole call: nothing changes, not its other
  designs or its tokens either, and the agent is told which designs, or that the modes, conflicted.
- **The token editor** says this before anything changes: "Every preview shows it at once. Saving the project writes it
  to src/index.css, and Undo takes it back." Its button is Apply.
- **A theme's value goes where the stylesheet keeps it** (PAR-468): the preview and the save find a theme's blocks by
  the rules the Tokens tab read it with (`themeOfSelector` in `packages/tokens/src/policy.ts`), so `dark` is `.dark`,
  `[data-theme="dark"]` or `html.dark` alike. Every block that declares the token gets the new value, so a later
  `[data-theme="dark"]` can't win back over an edited `.dark` after a save; a value the theme lacks goes into its first
  block, else a new `.dark`. A `:root` inside a `prefers-color-scheme` block is that scheme's theme and one inside any
  other `@media` is no theme's, so editing the default never changes either.
- **A `prefers-color-scheme` block is a theme** (PAR-138): `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` around the root is the
  `dark` theme, and a `light` one the default, in the Tokens tab as in `parity lib`. mantine's dark values are its
  `dark` theme and its light ones stay the defaults. A theme's own selector beats the block, so a `.dark` value wins
  over it. A dark value is previewed and saved in the block, and one the theme lacks is added to it. Every frame shares
  Parity's window, and with it one colour scheme, so frames draw the block as rules for their body's
  `data-canvas-color-scheme` (`prepareCanvasCss` in `packages/core/src/css.ts`). A frame gets `dark` when its mode's
  classes include `dark`, as the default Dark option's do, and `light` otherwise (`frameAttributes`), so a Light frame
  stays light when Parity's window is dark. A block nested in a rule, as Tailwind's `dark:` variant writes, is drawn the
  same way. A query that asks for more, such as `screen and (prefers-color-scheme: dark)`, is no theme and still follows
  Parity's window.
- **A frame shows a theme set by attribute** (PAR-22): a mode whose class names a theme the stylesheet switches on with
  an attribute, such as the default Dark option's `dark` with `[data-theme="dark"]`, sets that attribute on the frame's
  body too (`themeAttributes` and `frameAttributes` in `packages/tokens/src/policy.ts`, used by `frameSetup` in
  `apps/desktop/src/renderer/frame-setup.ts` for the canvas's frames and the offscreen page's). An attribute the mode
  sets itself wins. A theme's attribute on the root (`:root[data-theme="dark"]`) is set this way too (PAR-896), since
  frames draw that rule on their body as well, as below.
- **A frame draws the root with a class or attribute on it** (PAR-819): `:root.dark`, `html[data-theme=dark]` and
  `:root:not(.dark)` apply in frames as in a page. The frame's root is its shadow host, which matches nothing written
  after `:host`, only inside `:host()`, so `prepareCanvasCss` draws such a rule as two selectors: the host with it
  (`:host(.dark)`), where a decorator may set attributes, and the frame's body with it (`[data-canvas-body].dark`),
  where a mode's class goes. On the body, the root's own rule sits in a cascade layer the frame declares before the
  project's (`qualifiedRootLayer`), so the body's own rules beat it, as they beat what a page's body inherits from its
  root, while `:root.dark.contrast` still beats `:root.dark`. A font size there, in a nested `@media` too, sets the
  frame's `rem`, whatever the body's own font size is, and its `!important` is dropped there, as an inherited value has
  none. Left as is: a qualified root's value beats a plain root's on the body even where the page's cascade would pick
  the plain one, as with a `:root.dark` in an earlier layer than `:root`. A `var()` in its values resolves on the body,
  so a `body` rule that changes a variable the root's value refers to changes that value too, where a page's body would
  inherit it as the root worked it out. A root with a `:not()` on it is drawn as the body alone, since the host never
  has the mode's class. Tokens are read with the rule as written (`qualifiedRoots: false`), so `:root.dark` is still the
  `dark` theme in the Tokens tab, and now the Dark frame draws those values too.

### One undo step per gesture (PAR-441)

A gesture is one undo step, however long it takes and however many changes it makes: a design or note dragged by its
board, a layer drag, a resize handle, a scrub of a field's label, and a run of arrow presses, on the canvas or in a
field. Time plays no part, so a slow drag with long pauses is still one step, and two quick edits are two.

- **How a gesture says so.** Its source begins a gesture when it starts, passes it with each change it makes, and ends
  it when it's over. The changes join one step while it's the latest, labelled by the first of them (Undo resize layer).
- **Where each begins and ends.** A resize, a layer drag and a design dragged by its title begin their gesture as the
  press becomes a drag, 4 pixels from where it was pressed, and end it however the drag ends, as "Cursors and Escape
  during a gesture" sets out (PAR-568). A resize writes as it moves, and Escape takes it all back. A layer drag in a
  layout writes on the drop; an absolutely placed layer writes as it moves, and Escape takes that back too, as do the
  pointer cancelled and the window losing focus. Dragged by its title, a design writes once, when the drag ends. A
  design or note dragged by its board is tldraw's translate, from its first move until tldraw stops translating. A scrub
  runs from the press on the label to the release. A run of arrow presses on the canvas lasts while the same layers,
  designs or note stay selected, in whatever order, and nothing else changes: another edit, an undo or a redo, or
  selecting something else, also back to what it was, ends it. In a field, typing, Enter, Escape, leaving the field,
  scrubbing it or another selection ends a run of Up and Down, and Escape takes the run back to a checkpoint taken at
  its first press. A drag inside one of the Design tab's controls, such as a color's strip, is a run of its own, which
  Escape takes back too. Both kinds of run are a `GestureRun`, keyed by the selection's `selectionKey`, so a press on
  another selection starts a run of its own.
- **Gestures that change nothing.** A gesture that changes nothing adds no step, and one that comes back where it began,
  such as a drag back to its start or a nudge there and back, leaves none, with the file clean again and Redo as it was
  before the gesture.
- **Changes from elsewhere.** An agent's call or a file reloaded during a gesture is a step of its own, so the gesture's
  changes after it make a second step. The agent's work stays out of the gesture's undo.

Code: the `ProjectDoc` in `packages/multiplayer/src/project-doc.ts`: `beginGesture`, `transact` with the `gesture`
option, `endGesture`, `cancelGesture`, and `checkpoint` and `revert` by gesture. A gesture's step holds only its own
transactions, and undoing it applies their inverse operations in reverse order. The canvas's drags and runs begin and
end theirs through `canvas/gesture.ts`: `followPress` for resize handles (`canvas/CanvasOverlay.tsx`), layer drags
(`canvas/layer-drag.ts`) and title drags (`canvas/ContainerUtil.tsx`), and `GestureRun` for runs, in `canvas/nudge.ts`
(`runGesture`) and `inspector/sections/section-edits.ts` (the style sections' runs, as
`inspector/controls/edit-session.ts` says). A number prop's runs are gestures of its own (`NumberProp` in
`inspector/controls/number-field.tsx`). Their gesture reaches the document through `style-editor.ts`, `LayerPanel.tsx`
and `inspector/sections/PropsSection.tsx`. tldraw's translate is `canvas/CanvasEditor.tsx`'s.

### Edits in the state and variant shown (PAR-164)

The inspector's Editing control says where edits go on a component: in the base state ("Editing Default changes every
state") they change the design; in another state, or with a variant other than the default shown on its board, they're
kept as that state's or variant's changes ("changes only this state", "changes only the Large variant"). A screen has no
states, so it has no Editing control and its edits always change the design (PAR-1002).

- **Edits start from what the board shows.** The inspector, the text editor and Hide read a layer as the board draws it
  in the state being edited: with the variant shown, the state's changes, and the params it binds. The text editor opens
  on the state's text, not the base state's. Hide or show (Ctrl+Shift+H, or Hide and Show on a row in Layers, which runs
  the same command, PAR-586) hides what the state shows and shows what it hides, so a layer the state, the variant or a
  param hides counts as hidden, and Layers marks it so. The canvas menu's Hide says Show by the same reading
  (`hiddenOnBoard`, PAR-486), so it never offers to hide a layer the variant already hides.
- **Hide and Show land where the board's edits land** (PAR-497). In the base state, with a variant option other than the
  default shown, the change goes to that option; in any other state the state takes it. The row's menu used to name it
  (Show in Compact) and now says just Hide or Show (PAR-192). Core's `editTargetName` still names where an edit lands
  for the note above edits that always change the design.
- **Operations read what the frame shows** (PAR-464). Align, Wrap, resizing, nudging, dragging, Copy, Copy style, Paste
  style, Paste over, Paste to replace, Paste here and Select matching read a layer through core's evaluation, as
  `@parity-app/editor`'s `shownNode` and `boardReader` give it: the state being edited, the variant options the board
  shows, each bound param's value, and the responsive patches of the frame the layer was picked in, when one is known.
  Where they write doesn't change: an edit still lands in the state, or the variant, the Editing control names. The
  inspector reads the board without a viewport, as the text editor and Hide do, since its edits change the design or the
  state rather than a viewport's patch.
- **One rule says which design, state and viewport an edit lands on** (PAR-570). `@parity-app/editor`'s `editFrame`
  takes what was picked (a selection, a hit on the canvas, a layer's resize handles or the text being edited) and gives
  its design, the state it was picked in, and the viewport of that frame's mode. When the state picked is gone, or none
  was, it's the state the board shows. A design picked whole edits its base styles, a mode column its mode's viewport,
  and several designs the one picked last; a note or nothing has none. The text editor reads and writes through it, so
  it can't show one state's text and save into another. Before, the inspector, the canvas menu, nudging and Select
  matching each had a copy of the state rule, and the text editor wrote by one of its own.
- **The style rows read and write one way** (PAR-567). One layer, several layers, a layer inside an instance and the
  inspector's stories all go through `@parity-app/editor`'s `styleSelection`, so each reads its layers and the layout
  they sit in as the board shows them, with the variant shown, and its edits and resets land in the state or variant
  option the Editing control names. A row's reset takes back every key its edit writes: resetting Placement in a state
  drops the insets it set, and resetting Width drops the `grow` it replaced.
- **A component's board shows its params' defaults,** as an instance that sets none of them does. Changing a bound text
  or prop on the board, in the base state, changes the param's default too, so the board and the instances that don't
  set the param follow it: renaming the Stat card's Revenue label to Sales on the board makes `label` default to Sales.
  A param without a default follows the layer's own value, as before, and variants are picked in the title bar.
- **A state's change is kept against the board:** showing the Stat card's hidden Falling icon in Loading keeps
  `hidden: false` for Loading, which used to be dropped as matching the design.
- **Edits that always change the design say so first.** An image's file, alt text and fit, and an instance's Reset all,
  Swap and Detach can't differ by state. While the Editing control points at another state or a variant, a note above
  them, tinted as the Editing control is, says so: "File, alt text and fit change the design in every state, not only
  Loading." or "Reset all, Swap and Detach change the design in every variant, not only Large." In the base state
  there's nothing to say, so it doesn't show.
- **Values keep their types.** A param's or prop's field is chosen by what it's declared to take, not by the value it
  has: a number param with no value yet gets a number field, so typing 12 gives 12 and not "12"; a boolean gets a
  switch; text gets text. An object prop takes JSON, and JSON that doesn't parse stays in the field with "Can't read
  this as JSON: check its quotes, commas and brackets" under it, changing nothing, where it used to become a string. A
  prop of any type reads JSON when what's typed is JSON, and text otherwise. The instance's params, a component design's
  param defaults and component props all work this way.
- **Clearing a prop in a state turns it off there** (PAR-421). A switch turned back to its default, a text emptied or an
  attribute removed takes the prop away in the state being edited, so a prop the base design turns on can be off in one
  state: Button's button, disabled in the base, enabled in Outline. The field is marked as changed, an attribute taken
  away stays listed, and Reset takes the state's change back. An instance's param cleared in a state goes back to its
  default there. In the base state, clearing removes the prop from the design, as before.

### Only a component has states (PAR-1002)

States such as Default, Hover or Loading belong to a component design. A screen or a frame is drawn as its layers are,
so the project file refuses `states` on one, and a screen's board has no States menu and its layers no Editing control.
An instance has no State picker either: a copy always shows its component's base state, under its own overrides. A
screen that needs a component to look another way sets the component's params in the instance.

- **Turning a component into a screen keeps its base state's look.** What the base state changes moves into the screen's
  layers, the other states are dropped, and a notice names them ("Removed 2 states: Hover and Pressed") with Undo.
  Turning a screen into a component changes only its kind, and the component starts with its base state alone.
- **A component that lists no states has its base state, Default.** Code that reads a design's states goes through
  core's `designStates`, which gives a screen that one base state too, so selection, the canvas and the edit frame treat
  every design alike.
- **A component with one state lists it alone,** with no mark for which is shown and no Show every state, as there's
  nothing to pick between or show beside it. Adding a state brings both back.
- **Variants aren't in a component's Design tab for now.** Its Props lists params and slots; a variant a file already
  has still draws, and still shows on its instances. PAR-1017 brings variants back as Figma's work.
- **The agent can tell from the data.** `Designs()` lists `states` and `showing.state` only for components. `AddState`,
  `UpdateState` and `DeleteState` take a component, and those, Get, Update or Screenshot with a state, and
  `UpdateDesign`'s `state` or `allStates`, on a screen fail with "Home is a screen, and only a component has states."
  and the `invalid_input` code. The base state's id is still accepted on any design, so a screenshot of a screen in
  "default" works.

Code: `packages/core/src/document.ts` (`checkNoStates`, `baseState`, `designStates`), `edit.ts`
(`refuseUnlessComponent`), `render.ts` (an instance's scope in its component's base state);
`packages/editor/src/kinds.ts` (`withoutStates`) and `document-equality.ts` (a screen's view keeps no state);
`packages/agent/src/workspace.ts` (`listDesigns`, `namedState`) and `snippet-api.ts` (`ScreenSummary`,
`ComponentSummary`); in the app, `chrome/DesignPanel.tsx`, `chrome/LayerPanel.tsx` (`ComponentStateSelector`),
`canvas/BoardMenus.tsx` (the States menu) and `chrome/designs.ts` with `convert-to-frame.ts` (`droppedStatesLine`).

### A design's modes in its own order (PAR-923)

A screen's or component's board lists every mode of the project in the design's own order, in its title's Modes menu
(see "A board's rows and columns, in order"). The first one shown is drawn first on its board, and the other shown modes
beside it in that order. The Design tab has no Modes section: modes are set on the canvas (PAR-1071).

- **Each row has a handle** on the left, which drags it into place with the motion lists use, and Up and Down on it move
  it a place. A project with one mode has no handle.
- **Any mode can be off** while another shows. The one left showing can't be switched off, and its switch's hint says
  "At least one mode always shows". Turning off the first mode in the list makes the next one shown the first, and the
  list keeps its order.
- **No crown, radio, Show all or Only.** The project's primary mode isn't marked in the list or on a board's mode
  captions.
- **The file keeps the order** as the view's `order`, the modes' ids, with modes it doesn't name after it in project
  order, and the first frame's mode as `mode`, as before. An order that is the project's, with its first mode shown
  first, and a first mode that is the project's primary mode, aren't written down.
- **Each frame beside the first fits to at most 640 wide** (`companionScale`) unless its header's Zoom field sets it
  otherwise (see "A preview's header, settings and width"). A view's `scales`, by mode id, still applies where a preview
  sets no zoom of its own (`besideScale`), and the board's size follows them (`boardSize`).

Code: `packages/core/src/document.ts` (the view's `order` and `scales`), `modes.ts` (`shownModes`'s `ordered`) and
`board.ts` (`besideScale`); `packages/editor/src/document-equality.ts` (an empty order is dropped); in the app,
`canvas/view.ts` (`withModes`), `ModesList` in `canvas/view-lists.tsx`, `ShowList` in `chrome/ShowList.tsx`, the
`panelTable` in `packages/editor/src/layer-capabilities.ts` (no Modes section), and `canvas/ContainerView.tsx` (the
headers).

  fit".

### Unsaved changes survive a crash (PAR-905)

A crash, a forced quit or an agent stopping Parity no longer loses unsaved changes. Agents can't save, so long agent
runs build up a lot of them between the person's saves.

- **A recovery copy is kept** about a second after the changes change, while any are unsaved: each unsaved `.par` as it
  is on the canvas, the modes when they changed, and token values the stylesheet doesn't have yet. It's kept in Parity's
  app data, `<userData>/recovery/<hash of the project's folder>.json`, never in the project. The project service writes
  it, beside a temporary file it renames over the copy.
- **It's removed once nothing is unsaved:** after Save, after undoing back to what the files hold, when it closes, and
  when quitting after Save or Don't save. A clean quit leaves no copy, so nothing is offered next time.
- **The next open offers it back.** As the project opens, from the last session or by hand, "Restore unsaved changes?"
  says when the changes were made ("Parity closed before you saved your changes at 6:35 PM today") and offers Discard
  and Restore. Restore is focused; Escape and clicking away do nothing. Restore puts the changes back as one undo step,
  "Restore unsaved changes", unsaved, so the project's name shows its dot, Save writes them and Undo goes back to what
  the files hold. It goes over whatever the files hold now without asking, since an agent often changes a file with the
  CLI in between. Discard removes the copy. Projects that open together are asked about one after another. Nothing is
  kept for the project until it's answered, so the copy can't be written over first.
- **A copy in another's live room keeps none (PAR-1289).** The copy that writes the files has the room's edits, so a
  guest that quits unexpectedly isn't offered them as its own next time, which would bring older edits back into the
  room. A guest isn't offered the copy from last time either, and doesn't remove it, even after taking over the room's
  files: it waits for the project to open alone, unless the guest keeps its own over it.

Tests:

- `packages/editor/src/recovery.test.ts` (8): nothing kept while everything's saved or undone back; each unsaved file,
  the modes and token edits kept; restoring as one unsaved undo step, tokens with what the stylesheet holds, files made
  and deleted, and over a file an agent changed since; reading a copy back, and nothing from one that isn't.
- `apps/desktop/src/renderer/recovery.test.ts` (7): nothing written before the offer is answered, one write after a run
  of changes, removed after Save, brought up to date at once as the app quits, removed when discarded, and nothing kept
  or removed in a copy that joined another's room, nor after it takes over.
- `apps/desktop/src/utility/recovery.test.ts` (4): a file per project outside it, removed when there's nothing to keep,
  nothing read from a copy cut short or from another version, nothing kept without a folder.
- `apps/desktop/src/renderer/chrome/report-time.test.ts`: how the time reads ("6:35 PM today").
- `chrome/RestorePrompt.stories.tsx`: Offered, Restored (the dot after the project's name, and the undo step) and
  Discarded.

### Settings saved with the project (PAR-1085)

A project can keep settings of its own in its main `.par`, so everyone who opens it gets them. Settings' project page
lists them.

- **Its own preferences.** Autosave, snapping, the layout grid and the export sizes can be set for the project, in
  `preferences`, as `{ "snapping": false }`. The project's value wins over the person's while it's open, in its canvas,
  its menus and its Export section, and autosave follows each project's own. They're kept in the order they were set,
  which is the order the page lists them; changing one keeps its place.
- **Extensions' project settings,** in `extensions`, by the extension's prefix and then key, as
  `{ "storybook": { "configDir": "apps/web/.storybook" } }`. Each extension reads its own and takes one it can't read as
  its default; its manifest declares them (see [extensions.md](extensions.md#settings)). The window sends the field to
  the project service whenever it changes, saved or not, so extensions see it at once, and an extension's
  `parity.settings.update` comes back to the window as an undo step (PAR-1090).
- **Each change is an undo step** on the main file, such as "Set snapping for the project" or "Use your own snapping",
  saved by Save, or a moment later with autosave on, as any edit is. A project with no `.par` yet gets one. Clearing the
  last value takes the field out of the file, so a project that sets nothing keeps the file it had.
- **The View menu's Layout grid and Snap toggles, Search actions and the Export section change the value in effect:**
  the project's when it sets one, as an undo step, and the person's otherwise. What they show is what they change.
- **A value that doesn't fit is refused** when the file is read, as any field is: a preference a project can't set, or a
  value of the wrong type, such as an empty list of export sizes. Save a copy keeps the main file's settings.

Code: the schema and `preferenceOverrides`, `withProjectPreferences`, `setPreferenceOverride`,
`clearPreferenceOverride`, `setExtensionSetting` and `clearExtensionSetting` in `packages/core/src/project-settings.ts`,
which take and return data; `mergedDocument` in `packages/editor/src/snapshot.ts`; and in the window,
`renderer/project-settings.ts`: `useProjectSettings`, `setProjectPreference`, `clearProjectPreference`,
`setProjectExtensionSetting`, `clearProjectExtensionSetting`, `useEffectivePreferences`, `getEffectivePreferences` and
`setEffectivePreference`. An extension reads its own project settings, as Storybook does its config folder.

### A live room (PAR-1179, PAR-1270)

Copies of the app can edit one project together, each showing the others' pointers, selections, drags and agents. Rooms
across machines don't exist yet, so it's for trying multiplayer on one machine. It's the Multiplayer extension
(`@parity-app/extension-multiplayer`), an internal extension with a window module and a Node half, and it's off until
the **Live room** setting is on (Settings → Extensions → Multiplayer, an app setting, `multiplayer.liveRoom`).

Two copies on one machine, sharing their settings through one user data folder so the setting reaches both:

```bash
PARITY_USER_DATA=/tmp/parity-room PARITY_ROOM_NAME=Andrew pnpm dev
```

```bash
PARITY_USER_DATA=/tmp/parity-room PARITY_ROOM_NAME=Mia PARITY_UI_PORT=5311 PARITY_DEBUG_PORT=9334 pnpm dev
```

Turn on Live room in the first, then start the second. `PARITY_ROOM_NAME` names each copy's pointer; without it, it's
the signed-in person's first name.

- **Turning it on or off.** Turning the setting on reopens open projects in the room. Turning it off leaves the room:
  the document stays open with every change and its undo, this copy writes files and saves what differs, and a toast
  says "Left the live room". Turning it on again reopens the project in the room. A copy that finds it holds another
  version of the project than the room leaves the same way.
- **A room per project.** The Node half starts a relay on `127.0.0.1:5390`, or finds the one another copy started. Each
  project tab joins its project's room, keyed by the project's folder. The relay stops with the copy that started it, as
  when that copy closes the project: the others start it again, and the first back hosts and writes files.
- **The first copy in hosts.** Window modules start before the project's document opens (PAR-1267), so the extension
  says how it opens through `parity.sync`. The host opens the files in a new Loro document. A later copy opens on a
  snapshot, asked of the copies already there, so it starts from the same document, unsaved edits included. When the
  host leaves, the copy that joined next takes over. A copy that becomes host before its document is open, as when the
  host leaves just after sending the snapshot, turns file writes on once it's open (PAR-1281).
- **Joining shows.** While the project waits for the room, its opening screen adds the step "Joining the live room",
  with "If no one answers, it opens without the room." under the steps (PAR-1276). It waits for the relay and, for a
  copy that isn't hosting, the host's snapshot, up to 25 s, then opens alone.
- **Edits merge.** Each copy sends the changes it commits, repairs included, and takes in the others', which show as
  `remote` changes: in neither person's undo. A copy that finds a gap asks the host for what it's missing. One whose
  connection comes back asks both ways: the host sends what it missed and asks in turn for what the copy sent while it
  was cut off, so those edits reach the copy writing files. Token values merge a token at a time, and text is written as
  it's typed (PAR-1230).
- **Only the host writes files** (PAR-1231). It writes the others' edits like its own, autosaving them on its usual
  delay, and writes the stylesheet. A copy that doesn't write files has nothing to save: its name shows no unsaved dot,
  closing it asks nothing, and Save says "Saved by the room". Only the host takes in a file changed on disk; the others
  ignore their own disk, recording it once per file (`sync.diskIgnored`), but take the file as what's saved (PAR-1254).
  When one takes over, it writes every file that differs from what it last read from disk, when it opened or as the host
  saved it since, and every token value edited: it can't tell which the host saved to the stylesheet, so it writes them
  all. Its document comes from the room, which doesn't keep the order of a design's props or params, but it writes each
  file in the order the file has on disk, as every save does, so the diff shows only its edits (PAR-1288).
- **A copy that joins shows the room's token values,** compared with the stylesheet it loaded, not the edits' originals,
  so a value the host saved and changed back shows as the room has it (PAR-1254).
- **Everyone sees the same state and mode** (PAR-1231): which state and mode a design shows is an edit like any other.
- **People.** Each person is drawn in the palette the host assigned them, so they're the same color in every copy, and
  colors never run out (`parity.colors.assign`). Their pointer glides between the positions sent, with a badge of their
  first name, and stays where it was, faded, when they leave the canvas. What they've selected, and the text they're
  typing in, is outlined in their color with their name, with their caret where they're typing (PAR-1275). Their marquee
  shows as they drag it. A drag shows through `parity.canvas.preview`, with the lift, carry and settle of a local drag
  (PAR-1199), and settles on its write.
- **Coming back.** A copy whose connection to the relay comes back drops everyone who left meanwhile as if it had heard
  them leave: their pointer, a drag they were showing, following them, and their color (PAR-1282).
- **Who's here.** The avatar stack sits on the zoom controls' row, just left of them and as tall, with everyone in one
  overlapping stack, your own face first (PAR-1293). On a canvas narrower than 676px it moves below zoom. Following's
  banner, and the others at the top centre, sit under that row on a canvas narrower than 1040px, to keep clear of it. A
  face opens the person's card, with **Follow** and **Go to**. Following keeps the camera on what they see, with a frame
  and banner, until Esc, a pan or zoom, Stop, or they leave; a note then says why it ended.
- **Agents.** This copy's agents' steps go to the room, and steps from the room go to `parity.agents.receive`, so agent
  presence, where it's on, draws every copy's agents. The host numbers agents' colors as it does people's, by copy and
  agent, so an agent is the same color in every copy (PAR-1277). Each copy assigns the numbers under the keys agent
  presence claims colors with (`parity.colors.agents.assign`): the agent's id for its own agents, `copy:agentId` for
  another copy's.
- **In order, coalesced.** Changes, gestures, agents' steps and the host's colors go in order, one batch on its way at a
  time; presence goes with them, only the latest kept meanwhile. A move's write arrives before its end, so the preview
  settles on it, in the same batch or an earlier one.
- **Telemetry.** `room.relayStarted`, `room.joined`, `room.left`, `room.hostChanged`, `room.reconnected` and
  `room.latency`, recorded through `parity.telemetry`, beside core's `sync.*`.

Code: `packages/extension-multiplayer` (`window.tsx` wires the room, `room.ts` talks to the relay, `relay.ts` is the
relay, `people.ts` and `follow.ts` keep who's here and following, `agents.ts` the agents the host numbers, `hosting.ts`
file writes following the host, `layers.tsx` draws them); `startTabModules` in
`apps/desktop/src/renderer/window-modules.ts` and `joinRoom` and `setJoining` in `renderer/workspace.ts` (opening
through `parity.sync`, on Loro, and saying so in `ProjectStatus.tsx`); `openDocSession` in `renderer/project-doc.ts`
(the room's provider, and the saver writing files only while hosting); `setWritesFiles` and `written` in
`packages/multiplayer`'s saver; and `openLoro`'s `snapshot`, `subscribeLocalUpdates`, `pending` and tokens map in
`packages/multiplayer-loro`.

Tests:

- `packages/extension-multiplayer/src/room.test.ts`: who hosts and who's here, from the relay; one batch at a time, in
  order, with only the latest presence; the first snapshot opened on; another copy's events, presence and missing

- `packages/extension-multiplayer/src/people.test.ts`: colors kept and given out lowest first; each person's latest

- `packages/extension-multiplayer/src/agents.test.ts`: agents known by copy and id, forgotten with their copy, and kept

### The canvas surface: colors, the camera and boxes (PAR-1236)

Three core services that people's and agents' presence draws through, as docs/proposals/extensions-in-the-window.md sets
out. Internal extensions reach them through `parity.canvas` and `parity.colors` (PAR-1257). The project's canvas starts
its own as it mounts (`surfaceOf(editor)`).

- **Colors never run out.** People and agents get colors by key, never by color: `claim(key)` gives the lowest-numbered
  palette no other key in the project holds, a released number goes out again first, and past the hand-tuned palettes
  more are generated by number, the same in every copy. A room's numbers, given with `assign(key, n)`, win over claims,
  and a claim on a number the room gave someone else moves to a free one. Claims are counted per owner, an extension or
  `core`, and given back together when it stops. Agents at work get theirs this way, so a thirteenth agent gets a
  generated palette rather than sharing one. The first claim to need each generated palette records `colors.generated`.
- **The camera** says what's in view as a rect on the page, tells listeners at most once a frame, and `show(view)`
  glides there, fitted to the window within the canvas's zoom limits.
- **Following** keeps showing the views it's given, gliding to each. A view that comes while it glides changes where the
  glide ends rather than starting it again, and the same view again moves nothing, so a leader whose view comes with
  every pointer move is still reached. Its own moves are tagged, so only the person's end it: Esc, a pan (`panned`) or
  zoom (`zoomed`) of their own, or another page (`navigated`). The canvas's shortcuts offer Esc to the camera first
  (`escapeOnCanvas`), so it ends following and keeps the selection; with nothing followed it steps out of the selection
  as before. Another follow or `show` ends it as `replaced`, and its owner as `disposed`. A resized window fits what's
  followed again. Each ending records `follow.ended`. The frame and banner drawn while following are the Follow mode
  stories' (`Parity/Multiplayer/Follow mode`), drawn by whoever follows.
- **Boxes** say where a design's board, the frame a state and mode draws in, or a node in that frame is on the page,
  with its corner radius and its laid-out size in design pixels. With no frame in that state and mode, one in the mode
  is used, then the primary frame. A frame asleep, or a board culled out of view, gives the box to point at instead
  (`asleep`), and one not on the canvas says so (`missing`). Asked with `caret`, a node's box also says where a caret
  before that character of its text stands, when the text drawn reaches it (PAR-1275). `onBoxChange` checks once a frame
  while anyone listens, and a caret moving counts as a change. `hit` gives the design under a page point and the deepest
  node there, and `pageToScreen` and `screenToPage` convert between the page and the canvas area's pixels.

Code: `createColors` in `packages/presence-colors/src/colors.ts`; the camera, following and measuring policy in
`packages/editor/src/`: `canvas-surface.ts` (the shapes), `canvas-camera.ts` and `canvas-measure.ts`, each over a port;
and the window's side in `apps/desktop/src/renderer/canvas/surface/`: `colors.ts`, `camera-tldraw.ts`, `measure-dom.ts`
(which reads frames through `frame-geometry.ts`) and `index.ts`; `agent/agent-colors.ts`.

Tests:

- `packages/presence-colors/src/colors.test.ts` (6): the lowest free number, kept while claimed; forty agents without
  running out, `colors.generated` once per number; claims kept while any owner holds them and given back together; the
  room's numbers winning; keys the room assigned counted as holding a color; a number that isn't a palette's refused.
- `apps/desktop/src/renderer/agent/agent-colors.test.ts` (2): an agent keeps its palette; agents at once never share
  one, the hand-tuned ones first, and never run out.
- `packages/editor/src/canvas-camera.test.ts` (9): fitting a view within the zoom limits; gliding; telling a zoom from a
  pan; `show` gliding with listeners told once a frame; following through its own moves and ending on the person's pan
  or zoom; each other ending; arriving while told every frame, after each frame began, the same view or a moving one;
  fitting again on resize.
- `packages/editor/src/canvas-measure.test.ts` (7): the frame fallback; boards, frames and nodes; a sleeping frame and a
  culled board; changes told once a frame until disposed; a caret in a node's text only when asked and when the text
  reaches it, its moving told; hits on the deepest node.

### Presence components (PAR-1256)

How people and agents show on the canvas, in a package of their own, `@parity-app/presence-ui`, for the multiplayer and
agent presence extensions to render (docs/proposals/extensions-in-the-window.md, "What moves out of core"). They're the
approved Storybook designs (PAR-1188), made production components: they take who's here with each palette already
resolved, never a palette's name or key, and hold no room or editor logic. The stories under `Parity/Multiplayer/*` draw
them from the package.

- **Pointers.** A person's arrow with their first name, and a short note only when the room knows it for certain
  ("Typing…"); an agent's glows, and its badge has the icon for its step and what it says it's doing. Off the canvas a
  pointer stays where it was left, faded with only the name, and glides back from there when they return: for longer the
  further it is, from 280ms to 720ms, with positions arriving during the glide finishing it rather than restarting it.
  With reduced motion it jumps back, and an idle agent doesn't breathe.
- **Selections.** An outline in each person's color, several people on one layer a ring each with their name tags in a
  row, and a marquee in the color of whoever drags it. Layers rows show who else has a layer selected, and say so to a
  screen reader.
- **The avatar stack** beside the canvas's zoom: one stack, your own face first, then faces in the order people joined,
  each agent after whoever runs it, whoever you follow next and anyone away last; past the most it shows, a count that
  opens everyone. A face opens its card, with Follow and Go to, which closes once either starts (PAR-1291); your own
  opens yours, with Present to everyone and whether others' pointers show. Each action is a callback for the extension
  to answer.
- **Following.** The canvas framed in the leader's color and a banner with Stop, which names Esc. When following ends
  the banner says why: "Stopped following Mia", or "Mia left, so following stopped". Presenting, an invitation to follow
  and a dropped connection share the banner.

Code: `packages/presence-ui/src/`, with the glide in `glide.ts` and names, order and counts in `member.ts`. Agent
presence (`packages/extension-agent-presence`), the Multiplayer extension's layers
(`packages/extension-multiplayer/src/layers.tsx`) and carried pictures (`canvas/CarriedPicture.tsx`) draw with it
already. `useFollow`, which drives the Follow mode stories, stays with them; core's following is the camera's
(PAR-1236).

- `packages/presence-ui/src/glide.test.ts` (7): the glide's length by distance; the first position placed at once; steps
  in a straight line; staying put and fading off the canvas; gliding back for longer the further it is; positions during
  a glide finishing it; jumping back with reduced motion.
- `packages/presence-ui/src/member.test.ts` (11): first names and agents' whole names; whose an agent is; names in a
  sentence; initials by face size; ids telling namesakes apart; the line under a name; a palette's gradient; the stack's
  order, with whoever you follow first and an agent whose runner isn't here; how many faces show.

### Agents at work on the canvas (PAR-1269, PAR-1273, PAR-1274, PAR-1287, PAR-959)

Each agent working in a project has a pointer in its own colors that goes to what the agent reads or changes, at a pace
a person can follow. It's Parity's first internal extension, `@parity-app/extension-agent-presence`, with only a window
module (docs/proposals/extensions-in-the-window.md, "Agent presence"). Core keeps the agent API and reports each step
through `parity.agents`. The extension does the rest.

- **A pointer per agent.** It appears beside the first thing an agent looks at, travels there on a curve that lands with
  a small overshoot, and scans the target with a glow in the agent's colors. While the agent works it glances around the
  target. Between calls it stays near what it last looked at, breathing slowly, and after 20 seconds idle it fades and
  gives its color back. Its badge names the agent and has the icon for the step and the call's label. The strips that
  named each agent at the bottom left of the canvas are gone (PAR-959).
- **Moved boards.** When an agent moves a board, the board is held where it was as the step is told, before the write
  lands, and the pointer grabs it and drags it to where the agent put it. Core lets go of a hold after 10 seconds, so
  while a board waits the pointer plays as fast as it goes, and skips the oldest of the steps ahead that wouldn't leave
  it time to drag the board. A drag ends before the hold does. If the hold has all but run out when the move's turn
  comes, the board lands where the agent put it and the pointer looks at it there instead.
- **Keeping up.** Steps queue per agent, and the pointer stays close to what its agent is doing. When several are
  waiting it speeds up, to about a third of the time at most, and a long call keeps its first step and the latest 16. It
  also speeds up once a step has waited 3 seconds for its turn. Steps that waited longer than 6 seconds are skipped,
  except the latest, and a skipped move lands where the agent put it. A short call never plays for long after it ends:
  one that reads 60 layers in 1.8 seconds plays within 11.
- **A measurement** labels its target with its laid-out size while the pointer looks at it.
- **Other copies' agents** play the same way: steps passed in with a `from` are queued under `${from}:${agentId}`, the
  key their color is claimed under, so with multiplayer on everyone in a room sees every agent.
- **Show agents on canvas,** in Settings → Extensions → Agent presence, an app setting that starts on
  (`agentPresence.show`). Turned off, agents work as before and nothing draws them: their pointers go, and boards held
  for them are let go. Nothing else on the canvas changes.
- **With reduced motion** the pointer jumps instead of travelling and doesn't breathe, and scans don't sweep.

It draws in one `overSelection` page layer. Inside it, a pane covers what's in view at the screen's scale, moved with
the camera in the same frame as the page, so pointers, badges and scans stay the same size at any zoom. It finds where
to look with `canvas.box`: a layer in the frame of the step's state and mode, else the design's frame, else its board,
and the board itself for a move. A design key can hold a slash, so a layer's design is the longest key before a slash
that has a board. An asleep frame still gives a place to point at. It holds boards with `canvas.hold` and claims colors
with `useColor` from agents' palettes.

Code: `packages/extension-agent-presence/src/`: `window.tsx` (the module), `queue.ts` (the queue, holds and keys),
`AgentPresence.tsx` (the choreography), `targets.ts` (where to look), `motion.ts` (curves, pace and glances) and
`scanner.ts` (the scan's WebGL glow). Core's side is `renderer/agent/presence.ts` (the agent API's activity, with the
development room's steps told apart) and `windowAgentsPort` in `renderer/window-seams.ts`.

Tests:

- `packages/extension-agent-presence/src/queue.test.ts` (15): each agent's steps in order with a pointer until it
  retires; another copy's agents kept apart under their key; a moved board held while it's played and let go where it
  landed; moves left alone while nothing plays the queue; a long call trimmed, letting go of the boards it skips; a held
  board dragged, at the fastest pace until the pointer has it and while it drags it; the visits ahead of a held move
  skipped when they'd leave no time to drag it; a board let go where it was put once its hold has all but run out; every
  hold let go as it stops; listeners told as agents come and go; the board a move drags; a 1.8 s call of 60 reads played
  within 11 s; the visits that waited over 6 s skipped for the latest, a skipped board landing where it was put, several
  skipped moves of one board let go in order; the latest visit kept however long it waited, at the fastest pace.
- `packages/extension-agent-presence/src/targets.test.ts` (8): a page box on the screen; a layer in its state and mode's
  frame with its radius and size; falling back to the frame, then the board; a move by its board; an asleep frame; out
  of view, missing or naming no design skipped; a layer's design found when its key has a slash; staying put when the
  target goes.
- `packages/extension-agent-presence/src/window.test.ts` (3): running while its app setting, on to start with, is on;
  one layer over the selection, playing this copy's and other copies' agents alike; a board held as its step is told,
  and let go with the layer gone as it stops. Deactivating a window module as its setting goes off is
  `packages/extension-host/src/window-modules.test.ts`'s.
- `packages/extension-agent-presence/src/motion.test.ts`: easing, travel time, pace for a backlog and for how far behind

  `from`.

The stories under `Parity/Multiplayer/Agents/Behavior` play the extension's own queue and choreography over mock boards,
through a stand-in layer (`renderer/agent/story-layer.ts`), and `Parity/Multiplayer/Agents/On the canvas` runs the real
extension in the app's window.

Gaps: how long a visit and a grab take at the fastest pace is estimated (1.6 s and 1.2 s), not measured, so a slow frame
can still let a board land a moment early. The choreography's timing isn't unit tested; the stories are its check.

## Tokens

What the Tokens tab shows, and how a token is copied and edited from it.

### Previews of every kind of token (PAR-141)

Every row in the Tokens tab draws its token as it looks, in one fixed box, so the names line up whatever the kind. A
color shows a swatch for each theme; spacing, a bar at its true size; a radius, a rounded corner; a shadow, a card's
corner on the design's sheet; type, "Aa" in its size, weight, spacing or font; line height, lines of text; opacity and
blur, shapes on the design's sheet; a duration, a track; an easing, its curve; an animation, one plain block running its
keyframes; a z-index, where it falls among stacked sheets; breakpoints and containers, their share of a wide screen; an
aspect ratio, a box of that shape; a cursor, its icon, and hovering it shows the real cursor. A bare number has nothing
to draw, so its row shows the number. Beside the name is what the token comes to, in the unit people think in (`16px`,
`50%`, `1.5×`, the first font, `1000ms, loops`), or nothing where the preview says it all.

- **Sections follow what a token is for,** not where Parity files it: Colors (Semantic colors, then the Palette), Fonts,
  Font sizes, Font weights, Line height, Letter spacing, Spacing, Radius, Borders (Widths, Width and style), Shadows
  (Box, Inset, Drop, Text), Opacity, Blur (Layer, Backdrop), Motion (Durations, Easing, Animations), Layers,
  Breakpoints, Containers, Aspect ratios, Perspective, Cursors and Other. Effects and Other no longer hold blurs,
  z-indexes, border widths and the like. A token's kind comes from `previewKind` in `@parity-app/tokens`: its category,
  its name whatever its case or separators, its value, and the DTCG type a `.lib.par` gives it.
- **Values are what the token comes to.** A reference is followed to the value at the end, through `calc()` too, in each
  theme (`--radius-lg: calc(var(--radius) + 4px)` draws at 14px), and a step of the spacing scale is the scale times its
  factor. The project's custom properties are never set on Parity's own elements, since shadcn's names are Parity's too.
- **Spacing keeps the usual box.** A bar is drawn at its true size up to 16 pixels short of its box. Past that, a longer
  one is drawn true to there and the rest squeezed, hatched, into those last pixels, on a log scale up to 384 pixels, so
  a squeezed bar never passes for its true size and a longer length still ends further along; the pixels beside the name
  say how long it is. The detail draws the scale the same way with more room, so most steps are at their true size.
- **Every list of tokens shares one order** (`orderTokens` in `packages/tokens/src/token-order.ts`): the Tokens panel,
  the inspector's token pickers and the spacing picker all list from `TokenStore.inOrder`, and none sorts on its own, so
  they can't fall out of step (PAR-440). The store reads each token the way the panel draws it (`inTokenOrder` in
  `token-values.ts`): its kind from the DTCG type a `.lib.par` gives it, and its value as what it comes to, references
  and spacing steps filled in. A value of `none` counts as nothing, so it comes first. A length plain parsing can't
  read, such as `calc()`, is measured by the browser, in a shadow's layers too.
- **Each measured kind lists smallest first:** font weights from thin to black, font sizes from `text-xs` up, shadows by
  how far they reach past their box (for the furthest layer, the offset plus the blur and spread, read from the value
  rather than a size name), then spacing, radii, letter spacing, line heights, border widths, blurs, opacities,
  durations, layers, breakpoints, containers, perspective and aspect ratios by value, and animations by their duration.
  A value that is a duration is a duration whatever its name, so tw-animate-css's `animation-delay-75` lists with the
  durations. Tokens of the same value, and the kinds with no one order (colors, fonts, easings, cursors), go by name the
  way people count: numbers by value (`chart-2` before `chart-10`) and size words smallest first (`2xs`, `xs`, `sm`,
  `md`, `lg`, `xl`, `2xl`, and Fluent's `XXS` to `XXL` and `Small` to `XLarge`). A size word comes before any other word
  in the same place (`text-lg` before `text-normal`), so the order never runs in a circle. A value that can't be
  measured goes after the rest, by name the same way.
- **What a design shows sits on the design's sheet:** shadows, blur, opacity and type are drawn on white in the light
  theme, as in a frame, not on Parity's dark chrome. Measurements are diagrams in Parity's ink.
- **Every color swatch has one clean edge (PAR-435).** One element paints the color over a checkerboard, which shows
  through a see-through color, and draws a hairline over both in 14% of Parity's text color, following the swatch's
  radius (`swatch` in `token-previews.tsx`). It's light in the dark UI and dark in the light one, so black, white and
  `foreground`-like swatches stand off the panel, with no white corners on dark ones. Rows, tiles, the detail's preview
  and value dots (`Swatch` in `chrome/fields.tsx`, which the inspector's token picker shares), palette shades and a
  library's described tokens all draw it. A token has a swatch for each theme, split by a 1px gap, even where two themes
  share a value, in rows, tiles and the detail, whose swatches are each named for their theme. A palette row's last
  shade is rounded too: each shade's copy helper follows it in the row, so the rounding goes by the last button rather
  than the last element.
- **Tiles.** The List and Tiles buttons beside the search switch views. Tiles are two across, each a larger preview with
  the name and what it comes to under it. A bare number stays a row, as a tile of only a name says less. The palette
  stays a grid in both.
- **Folding.** Each section's title folds it, and again opens it; a folded section keeps its title and count. Starting
  or clearing a search unfolds every section, so nothing that matches is hidden.
- **Copying.** A click on a row or tile copies the token's name (`radius-md`), which Parity's fields take, and the row
  says Copied where its value was, for a moment, so the name never gives up room for a button. A detail a hover opened
  stays open through the click. Ctrl+C (Cmd+C on a Mac) on a row or tile does the same. A palette shade's tooltip is its
  name, and a click copies it, with a "Copied" bubble, as there's little else to do with one of 242.
- **Editing.** Resting the pointer on a row or tile opens the token's detail (below), as a component's card opens, and
  the right arrow opens it from the keyboard, or moves the keyboard into one a hover opened, past a disabled Edit. Edit
  in the detail changes the token. A palette shade is edited from a search: while searching, the palette's matches list
  as rows.
- **Motion plays only while it's looked at:** a duration, easing or animation runs while its row or tile is hovered or
  has the keyboard, through the Web Animations API, and stops when that ends, so an idle tab runs no animations. With
  reduced motion it holds still. An animation runs the project's own `@keyframes`, read by name from its stylesheet,
  inside `@layer` and `@media` too; one whose keyframes aren't there holds still. Every animation, whichever library
  it's from, runs on the same plain block, with a dashed outline where the block rests, so one that fades, shrinks or
  collapses still shows against where it was. A keyframe value reading a variable only its page has (Radix's
  `--radix-accordion-content-height`) takes the variable's fallback, or, for a size, the block's own.
- **Only the rows in view are drawn,** so the theme's 500 tokens cost what a screenful does. The search and the filters
  stay above the list as it scrolls.
- **Narrow panels.** The left panel is at least 232 pixels wide, enough for every tab's icon and the collapse button.
  The open tab shows its name only when the tab strip has room for it, and is otherwise an icon like the rest, with its
  name in the tooltip. The filters drop their counts before their names, and every count is in the filter's tooltip. The
  search says "Search tokens", without a count, which didn't fit (PAR-437).

### A token's detail (PAR-143)

Resting the pointer on a token's row or tile opens its detail beside the panel (the right arrow opens it from the
keyboard); a click on the row copies the token's name. The detail, top to bottom:

- **A large preview.** A color shows each theme side by side, named. A spacing step is drawn at its true size among up
  to eight of its neighbours on the scale; a duration races the others; an easing is drawn over the rest, faintly; a
  font or size is set in a specimen using “The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.” (PAR-499); a z-index is marked
  in its stack; a breakpoint on a ruler with phone, tablet and laptop widths. Motion plays while the detail is open,
  with a Pause button on the preview; with reduced motion it waits for Play.
- **The name** (`--primary`), with what it comes to on the right as its row shows it, left out where the value already
  says just that, and what a `.lib.par` says it's for.
- **One list of facts:** its value in each theme, a shadow's layers or a font stack one part to a line; Built on, the
  tokens its values refer to in any theme, each with what it comes to (a spacing step shows `spacing × 4`); and From,
  the library that describes it. A value the last save couldn't write says "Not written to the stylesheet".
- **A bar with Edit and Copy.** Copy copies the name, as rows do; its arrow opens Copy as, with `var()` under CSS and
  the name under Token. It offers nothing a framework adds, such as a class, since a variable says only that it can be
  used as one, whichever framework defined it. A spacing step has no value of its own, so its Edit is off, and its hint
  says to change `--spacing` instead.

Themes are named as the Modes panel names them: the root's values are the theme option that adds no class (Light), and
`.dark`'s are the option whose class is `dark` (Dark). A library's themes take their options' names too, and a theme no
option switches on is named from its key (`teams-high-contrast` is Teams high contrast). The class itself never shows.

Edit turns the values into fields in place, checked as they're typed, with what's wrong under the field: a bracket or
quote left open ("A bracket isn't closed. Add ) at the end."), which the browser would close by itself and take; a
`var()` naming no token ("There's no token named radius-huge."), each reference read in its own theme; a `var()` naming
the token itself ("primary can't be built on itself.") or one built on it ("primary is built on chart-1, so this would
loop."), in another `var()`'s fallback too, which the old values alone would let through; and a value that, with its
references filled in, isn't the kind's ("That isn't a color. Try oklch(0.6 0.2 250) or #2563eb."). The preview follows
what's typed while it can draw it. Apply is off until something changed and every value is right; Cancel or Escape in a
field leaves editing without changing anything, and Escape from the buttons closes the detail. Apply changes every frame
at once as one undoable step, unsaved, as any edit is (see "One history, saved together"): the detail then says
"Applied. Saving writes it to src/index.css.", with Undo while that's still the last step, even after Edit and Cancel.

Code: `apps/desktop/src/renderer/chrome/TokenDetail.tsx` (`TokenDetail`, `DetailPreview`, `themeLabel`, `CopyMenu`); the
panel's `TokenPopover` and `Detail` in `chrome/TokensPanel.tsx`, which name themes with `themeNamesOf` from the
project's modes and apply through `TokenStore.set`. What an edit may write is decided in `packages/tokens/src/checks.ts`
(PAR-569): `checkTokenEdit` gives each theme's problem and the smallest changes to save, from `loopProblem` and
`valueProblem`, with `builtOn` for the tokens another is built on; the detail passes in the browser's `CSS.supports`,
and keeps only the view. The agent's `SetTokens` passes `validate` from `@parity-app/style-schema` as it runs, which
checks the value against its property's grammar without a browser (PAR-940), then asks the window's browser once the
snippet ends. The Storybook exploration's own detail (`explorations/previews/token-panels.tsx`) is the design it came
from, with Save in place of Apply.

### Full round beside the radius tokens (PAR-458)

The radius field takes `radius-full` as well as the project's radius tokens. It's Tailwind's `rounded-full`, which
Tailwind writes as `calc(infinity * 1px)` rather than as a theme variable: the corners are as round as the box allows,
so a square of any size is a circle and a wider box is a pill, in every viewport. A frame draws it as
`var(--radius-full, calc(infinity * 1px))`, so a project that declares its own `--radius-full` keeps that value, and one
that doesn't gets no new variable. `GetTokens` (and `parity tokens`, MCP `get_tokens`) lists it after the tokens, as
`{ name: "radius-full", category: "radius", source: "keyword", values: { default: "calc(infinity * 1px)" } }`, unless
the project has a token of that name, which is listed instead. An agent's `borderRadius: { token: "radius-full" }`, in a
design, a viewport's patch or a state, gets no "isn't a token" warning; under any other key it's still not a token.

Code: `radiusKeywords` and `radiusCss` in `packages/core/src/render.ts`; `tokensAndKeywords` in

### The token nearest a raw value, for agents (PAR-833)

A design handed to an agent often has colors and sizes that aren't tokens, such as `#2f6fed` or `13px`. The skill tells
it never to write one raw, and `GetTokens({ nearest: "#2f6fed" })` (`parity tokens --nearest`, MCP `get_tokens`) says
what to write instead: the tokens that can be compared with the value, nearest first, each with its `distance`. It's the
hint PAR-186's styling controls give designers ("Nearest to 12px"), for agents.

- **Colors with colors, lengths with lengths.** A color is read from hex or `oklch()` and compared only with color
  tokens; a length in px, rem or em (16px to a rem) only with length tokens: spacing, radius, type size, tracking,
  border width, blur, breakpoints and containers. The other filters narrow it, so `category: "font-size"` keeps a `13px`
  to type sizes. Anything else, such as `blue` or a bare `13`, is refused as `invalid_input` on `nearest`.
- **How far.** A color's distance is OKLab's, with any difference in alpha added, to three decimals; under 0.02 looks
  the same. A length's is in pixels, to two decimals.
- **What a token comes to.** Each token is read in the default theme, or the one theme that sets it, with the tokens it
  refers to worked out and simple `calc()` done: `primary: var(--color-blue-600)` is that blue, `spacing-3` is 12px and
  `radius-md`'s `calc(var(--radius) - 2px)` is 8px. A token that can't be read that way, such as a color name, `clamp()`
  or `radius-full`'s infinity, is left out.
- **Ties go to the project's own tokens,** the semantic ones the skill prefers, then by name.
- **The warning says so too.** When a design names a color under `fills`, `color` or `borderColor`, or a length under
  `borderRadius`, `fontSize` or `letterSpacing`, its "isn't a token" warning names the call:
  `Use a name from GetTokens({ nearest: "#2f6fed", category: "color" }), which lists the nearest first.`

Code: `readNearValue` and `nearestTokens` in `packages/tokens/src/nearest.ts`, reading colors with `parseColor` in
`packages/tokens/src/color.ts` and lengths with `scaleValue` and `lengthKinds` in `token-order.ts`; `getTokens` in
`packages/agent/src/workspace.ts`; `nearestHint` in `packages/agent/src/lint.ts`; `describeTokens` in
`packages/cli/src/client.ts`.

Tests: `packages/tokens/src/nearest.test.ts` (reading values, colors through references, the same color written another

nearest a color or a length", and `nearest: "blue"` refused); `packages/agent/src/lint.test.ts` ("names the call that
lists the tokens nearest a raw color or length"); `packages/cli/src/client.test.ts` and `operations.test.ts` (the
printed order, and `--nearest` reaching the app as MCP's `nearest` does); the skill's example in `execute.md`, run by

its colors that way gets no nearest color; colors are compared in the default theme only.

### Adding a token, and a name that isn't one (PAR-911)

An agent's `SetTokens` adds a token as well as changing one, and a design that names a token the project doesn't have is
told what the project does have. Tokens come in through the styles adapter that read the stylesheet and go out through
the same one; nothing between knows the framework.

- **A new name is a new token.** `SetTokens({ "text-2xl": "1.5rem" })`, or `{ default: "…", dark: "…" }` for a value per
  theme, makes a token the project doesn't have, in the category its name and value say (`categorize`) and as one of the
  project's own (`source: "semantic"`). The rest of the call lists it in `GetTokens` and takes it in a style without a
  warning. It's an ordinary token edit: every frame draws it at once, the Tokens tab lists it before it's saved, Save
  writes it and Undo takes it back, out of the stylesheet too once it was saved.
- **Where Save writes it is the styles provider's call.** Its `writeTokens({ source, writes, theme })` writes values
  into a stylesheet's source where its framework keeps them. A project no provider handles has plain custom properties,
  which `writeTokenChanges` writes: a default value in the first `:root` under no condition, a theme's in the block the
  stylesheet gives that theme (`.dark`, `[data-theme="dark"]` or a `prefers-color-scheme` root), each made at the end of
  the file when there's none. Tailwind's extension puts a default value in `@theme` when the variable is in Tailwind's
  theme already or its name is in one of Tailwind's namespaces (`text-*`, `shadow-*`, `radius-*`, `color-*` and the
  rest), so the class exists, and hands every other value to the plain writer. A declaration that exists is edited where
  it is, whichever block that is.
- **The warning says what the project has.** A style key takes one category of token: `fontSize` a font size,
  `boxShadow` a shadow, `fills` a color. A name there that isn't a token gets one of these, in a design, a viewport's
  patch or a state alike:
  - `fontSize "text-2xl" isn't a token. The project's font-size tokens are text-xs, text-sm and text-base. Use one, or add text-2xl with SetTokens.`
    The tokens are listed smallest first while there are eight or fewer; past that it's
    `Use a name from GetTokens({ category: "color" }), or add pink with SetTokens.`
  - `boxShadow[0].token "shadow-md" isn't a token, and the project has no shadow tokens. Add shadow-md with SetTokens.`
  - A raw color or length keeps PAR-833's hint, the call that lists the nearest tokens, and a value that couldn't be a
    token's name (`0 1px 2px black`) isn't offered to `SetTokens` by name.
  - A place that takes more than one category (a gradient, a blur, a transition's duration or easing) keeps
    `Use a name from GetTokens().`

Code: `writeTokenChanges` and `writeCustomProperty` in `packages/tokens/src/stylesheet.ts`; `withTokenChanges` in
`packages/tokens/src/tokens.ts`; `writeTailwindTokens` in `packages/extension-tailwind/src/tokens.ts`; `StylesProvider`
in `packages/extension/src/api.ts`; `saveTokens` in `apps/desktop/src/utility/projects.ts`; `tokensNow` in
`packages/agent/src/workspace.ts` and `notAToken` in `packages/agent/src/lint.ts`; `tokensWithEdits` in
`packages/editor/src/token-edits.ts`.

Tests: `packages/extension-tailwind/src/tokens.test.ts` (5: a theme variable edited in its `@theme` block or a new one,
a new namespaced token in `@theme`, any other in the root and a theme's value in its block, a namespaced variable edited

## Accessibility

How the Accessibility tab checks a design and helps fix what it finds.

### Contrast fixes from the project's tokens (PAR-21)

Each contrast failure in the Accessibility tab suggests the project's color token closest to the text's color that
passes, drawn as a second text sample on the same background with the ratio it reaches ("Use `foreground`, Reaches
18.16:1"). Apply sets it as the layers' `color` as one undoable step named "Use foreground", then checks the design
again, since only a check shows the fix worked; the row offers Undo while that's still the last step, and Undo checks
again too. Undo from the keyboard leaves the check out of date instead. When no token passes on that background, the row
says so and has no Apply. `check_accessibility` and `Accessibility()` give agents the same fix on each contrast finding
(`contrast.fix`: the token, its color in that frame and its lowest ratio, or `"none"`), and `parity a11y` prints it as
the style to set.

- **Every frame counts, passing ones too.** The token must pass in every frame the layer's text was measured in,
  including frames where it passes now, so fixing light mode can't break dark. axe-core's passes for `color-contrast`
  give those frames' colors.
- **Closest means least change.** Distance is in OKLab, from the measured text color, added up over the frames. A
  token's own transparency is laid over the background first.
- **The project's own tokens first.** Semantic tokens (`foreground`, `primary`…) are tried before the framework's
  palette, so text that follows a theme still does; the palette is tried only when no semantic token passes.
- **Only where coloring the layer reaches the text.** The frame sets an unused color on the layer's element and sees
  whether the text takes it. Text colored inside a component, by its own classes, or inside an instance gets no fix,
  since setting the layer's color wouldn't change it.
- **Out of date, and checking again.** A check whose design changed since shows an amber warning with Check again, a dot
  on the refresh button, and its findings faded. Checking again keeps the last findings, faded, under "Checking again",
  rather than emptying the panel.
- **The project's checks.** The project keeps its designs' checks until it closes, when they go, and a check still
  running then is let go (PAR-1005).
- **The newest check wins.** Checking a design again before the last check answers shows only the newest check's result,
  whichever reply lands first; an older one's result or failure is dropped (PAR-979).

Code: `contrastFix` and `contrastRatio` in `packages/tokens/src/contrast.ts`, `colorDistance` in
`packages/tokens/src/color.ts`; the frame's readings (`contrastReadings`, `follows`, `tokenColors`) in
`apps/desktop/src/renderer/render.ts`; `addContrastFixes` in `packages/agent/src/frames.ts`; `ContrastFixRow`,
`ImpactTally` and `DesignCheck` in `apps/desktop/src/renderer/chrome/AccessibilityPanel.tsx`; the checks kept for each
tab, `checksOf` in `chrome/accessibility-checks.ts`; `fixLine` in `packages/cli/src/client.ts`.

Tests: `packages/tokens/src/contrast.test.ts` (WCAG ratios, translucent colors, the closest passing token, passing
frames, preferred tokens and the fallback, large text, no token); `packages/agent/src/run.test.ts` ("gives contrast
failures the token that passes in every frame", "gives no contrast fix when coloring the layer wouldn't reach its
text"); `packages/cli/src/client.test.ts` ("gives a contrast failure's fix as the style to set");
`apps/desktop/src/renderer/project-part.test.ts` (the checks forgotten when the project closes, and one running then let

landing first leaves it checking, and an older failure is dropped); and `chrome/AccessibilityPanel.stories.tsx`:
ContrastFix (Apply, the change, checking again), NoPassingToken, OutOfDate, CheckingAgain, ManyFindings (the tally) and
