## What the editor itself loads

What Parity's own UI costs the window, apart from the projects it shows.

### Icons and dependencies served lean (PAR-199)

The window loads only the lucide icons the editor uses, and Parity's dependencies minified. Nothing looks different; the
window holds less.

- **Icons:** each `import { … } from "lucide-react"` in the app's code is rewritten, while Vite serves it, to import
  each icon from its own file, and lucide-react is kept out of Vite's prebundling. Types are dropped, a name
  lucide-react doesn't export stays imported from the package so it fails as before, and the import keeps its lines, so
  the module's source map holds. Imports are found by parsing the module, so import-like text in a string stays.
  Dependencies and a project's own icons, which its builder serves, are left alone. Storybook uses the same config;
  builds bundle lucide-react as usual.
- **Dependencies:** what Vite prebundles for the UI is minified. Their source maps still lead DevTools to the code as
  published, so a stack trace through tldraw reads as before once DevTools maps it.
- **Measured** on the example project, against an isolated copy of the app: the window's scripts went from 19.3 M
  characters to 14.9 M, lucide-react's from 1.73 M to 0.28 M across 149 files, tldraw's from 3.53 M to 1.68 M, and the
  heap after a collection from 151 to about 141 MB.

Code: `iconImports` and `iconImportsPlugin` in `apps/desktop/scripts/icon-imports.ts`, and `optimizeDeps` in
`apps/desktop/vite.config.ts`.

Tests: `apps/desktop/scripts/icon-imports.test.ts` (8: every name an icon goes by, the installed package's index, one
file per icon under the module's own names, lines kept, types dropped, unknown names left, import-like text in strings
and comments left, other modules unchanged). The e2e suite (`pnpm test:app`) runs the editor with both in place. Gaps:
the minified prebundle has no test of its own; it was checked in an isolated copy of the app on 2026-10-29, where all
736 icons on screen drew and the window's scripts were measured over the DevTools protocol.

### React's production build on request (PAR-519, PAR-550)

`pnpm dev` runs Parity's window on React's development build, with StrictMode's checks, Fast Refresh and React's
warnings, as the daily driver. `pnpm dev:prod`, and the copy `pnpm perf` starts, run it on React's production build,
which is faster. The audit timed, by hand on the example project, selecting a design, committing a field and undo going
from 210 to 360 ms to the next paint to under 90, and opening the Components panel from 1.4 s to 0.14 s.

| `pnpm perf` on the example project              | Development build | Production build |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ----------------- | ---------------- |
| Select a design, median / max                   | 180 / 298 ms      | 71 / 126 ms      |
| Edit a design, median / max                     | 134 / 386 ms      | 47 / 117 ms      |
| Started again, usable (`--open-only`, two runs) | 9.4 and 4.4 s     | 2.7 and 3.0 s    |
| The window's memory                             | 764 MB            | 590 MB           |

On 2026-11-04, on Windows 11 with other sessions using the machine, which the development build's restart times show.
Started again after a full run's measuring, both builds took about 4.7 s.

- **The dev script takes the build as a flag,** `--react production`, which `pnpm dev:prod` passes, and starts the UI's
  Vite server in a mode of its own (`react-production`), which the UI's Vite config reads. No environment variable is
  involved. `pnpm perf` passes the flag too, unless it's run with `--react development`, and records the build in each
  result. Storybook and the end-to-end suite, which don't pass it, run the development build.
- **Dependencies are prebundled as production:** the UI's Vite config sets `process.env.NODE_ENV` to `production` in the
  dependency optimizer (Rolldown's `transform.define`), as Vite's extension does for frames (PAR-198). The app's own
  modules are still served as in development, so `import.meta.env.DEV` stays true.
- **The app's JSX calls the production `jsx`:** it's still compiled for development, calling `jsxDEV`, which the
  production build leaves out, so `react/jsx-dev-runtime` is aliased to `scripts/jsx-dev-runtime.ts`, React's `jsx`.
- **Fast Refresh is off,** since it reaches React only through the development build: a change to a component reloads
  the page, as a change to any other module already did.
- **The dev script prints which build it runs.** Development is the default.
- **tldraw still draws,** since the window is on localhost, where tldraw needs no licence key.
- **Switching builds rebuilds the prebundle:** Vite keys it by the optimizer's options and the aliases, so the other
  build's is never served.

Code: `reactFlag`, `reactBuild`, `reactProductionMode` and `reactBuildConfig` in `apps/desktop/scripts/react-build.ts`,
used by `apps/desktop/vite.config.ts`, `apps/desktop/scripts/dev.ts` and `apps/desktop/scripts/perf.ts`; `dev:prod` in
both `package.json` files.

Tests: `apps/desktop/scripts/react-build.test.ts` (8: the flag's values, an unknown one rejected, the flag taken out of
the arguments wherever it is, the flag without a value rejected, nothing added for the development build, the production
build's define, alias and Fast Refresh filter, the stand-in being React's `jsx`). Gaps: the window's build is checked by
hand, as the e2e suite runs the development build. On 2026-11-04, in an isolated copy, React's fibers had no development
fields on the production build and had them on the development build, tldraw drew the canvas on both, an edited
component reloaded the page on the production build, and the prebundle's config hash differed between the builds.

## Opening and closing projects

What opening a project loads into the window, and what closing it gives back.

On first launch the installed app shows the sign-in screen, and Home once you sign in or go on without (see
[Signing in](#signing-in-par-612)). Later launches reopen the project the window had open, or show Home if it had none.
Development can request an initial project through its runner. `workspace.test.ts` covers these startup choices (PAR-8,
PAR-605, PAR-1241).

### One project per window, and Home (PAR-1241, PAR-605, PAR-607, PAR-188)

A window holds one project, and shows Home when none is open, as
[lens-layout.md](proposals/lens-layout.md#one-project-at-a-time) has it. There are no project tabs, new tabs or tab bar.

- **The title bar** has the app's menus on the left, your account on the right, and the open project's name in the
  middle, with a dot after it while it has unsaved changes. The name's hint is the project's folder, with Unsaved
  changes under it when there are some. The name opens the project's menu: Open project folder…, the projects opened
  before under Recent, most recent first, and Close project. On Home the middle is empty.
- **Opening a project closes the open one,** however it's opened: the project's menu, File, Home, Search or
  `parity open`. One with unsaved changes asks first, as closing it does: "Save changes?", with Save and Don't save.
  Escape or clicking away keeps it open and opens nothing. Opening the project that's open leaves it as it is, and one
  that couldn't open opens again. A project still opening is closed too, and the service closes it once it has it (see A
  project closed while it opens).
- **Close project,** in the project's menu and File, or Ctrl+W, asks the same and leaves the window on Home. On Home
  it's unavailable.
- **An extension's page** shows in the project's place, under the title bar, with a button that closes it and shows the
  project again as it was (see Extensions' views). Closing the project closes its page.
- **Agents see the project as the one tab,** or none on Home: `parity tabs` lists it, a call naming another tab says
  which is open, and `parity open` opens a project in its place, failing if the person keeps the open one.
- **Home** has its workspace menu (see Signing in), then Search, Open and New project along the top. Below them, the
  Continue where you left off section offers the project opened last, which its picture, Resume or Enter opens, with For
  you beside it once you're signed in; signed out there's no For you. For you says nothing needs you, and what will show
  up there, until something can.
- **The first time (PAR-188),** before any project has opened, Home keeps that layout. Where this copy of Parity has the
  example, as it does run from the repository, Acme takes Continue's place: its picture, shipped with Parity until its
  own is kept, a line on what to try there, and Open Acme. Bring your own app sits beside it, with Open a folder and
  Open a project file. Without the example, the place shows what Parity does with your app, with the same two buttons.
- **Home lists your projects** as cards under Recent, Starred, Shared with you and All projects, two rows until Show N
  more, which sits beside the filters, or after the cards in a window as narrow as a phone. There Search spans the row
  under the workspace menu. A card has the project's picture, its folder's name and when it was last opened; its tooltip
  is the folder's path. Its menu opens it, stars or unstars it, copies its link and removes it from Recent. Recent
  leaves out the project Home offers to continue. A list with nothing in it says what will show up there, in a dashed
  box a row of cards tall.
- **A project whose folder is gone (PAR-188)** — moved, renamed, deleted, or on a drive that isn't plugged in — is
  greyed, with Folder not found on its picture and under its name. Continue offers the next one instead, and opening it
  says where the folder was and offers Remove. It stays listed until removed, since a drive comes back. The service
  checks the listed folders when the window starts, when the list changes, and each time the project closes and Home
  shows.
- **Every copy of Parity lists the same projects,** kept in `projects.json` in the app's data folder. Opening, starring
  or removing a project in one copy changes Home in the others within a moment, and a change two copies make at once
  keeps both.
- **The project comes back next time,** kept in `state.json` with the panel layout and Search's recent picks. Each
  window's project has an entry of its own, which main writes as it changes and every 10 seconds, so a copy that crashed
  loses nothing: the next copy to start reopens the project of the newest copy that's gone, and a window that reloads
  keeps its own. A window closed on Home keeps none. A window from before PAR-1241 kept several projects; the next one
  reopens the one it showed. A copy started for one project, as `pnpm dev` is, opens that project and keeps none. The
  layout is the one last saved by any copy; a running copy doesn't follow another's.
- **Search is Ctrl+K,** which lists your projects as well as actions: first on Home, last in a project.
- **A project's picture is its canvas as last saved (PAR-607).** It shows the project's first screens as the canvas drew
  them, each its main frame with the phone frame beside it where its board shows one, each frame the shape of its
  window, or shorter where the frame is. Moving the pointer across a card flips through them, naming each; Home's
  Continue picture names the frames above them, as the canvas does. Up to five screens are pictured: those with a phone
  frame beside them first, then the rest, each in Layers' order; components and frames aren't. A project not opened
  since shows a placeholder, a board and a phone in a color of its own with its initial. Each frame has a mid-grey edge,
  so a phone over a desktop frame shows against it whether their screens are light or dark, and the phone frame has a
  shadow of its own, so it stands off the main frame it overlaps.
  - **When it's taken:** two seconds after the project opens and after each save, once the canvas has drawn the frames
    and has every bitmap it's waiting for, from those bitmaps; no frame is drawn again for it. A run of saves takes one.
    Edits not saved yet are never pictured: a picture that would show them waits for the next save. A code change, the
    guest moving or the service restarting doesn't take it again, since the project stays the same session until it
    closes; reopening it does (PAR-1004).
  - **Where it's kept:** in Parity's app data, in `pictures`, one file per project with each frame cut to the top of its
    window, about 70 KB for the example's five screens. Clear bitmap cache leaves them. A project's picture goes when
    Home stops listing it.
- **Stubs:** For you and Shared with you are empty; New project, cloning, Copy link, Invite people and New organization
  show a toast saying they aren't available yet. New project's and cloning's toasts also offer Open folder. A project's
  menu has no New project from this until projects can be made (PAR-284).

### The project's lenses (PAR-1243)

The open project shows in the lens shell, as [lens-layout.md](proposals/lens-layout.md#lenses-down-the-left) has it: the
lens bar down the window's left edge, each open lens a tab over its canvas, and the left panel and inspector of the lens
in focus beside them, over the status bar. The title bar stays above, as on Home.

- **Pages and Screens are the lenses so far,** and the lens bar lists only lenses that are built. Screens is today's
  canvas, Layers with its asset tabs, and the inspector with Modes: it draws the designs, stories and component boards
  until Stories and Components have lenses of their own. Pages has a canvas of its own (see Pages, a lens of its own).
  Opening a project shows Screens.
- **Each lens has a canvas of its own,** a tldraw editor drawing its part of the project. The project holds the editor
  of the lens in focus, which Layers, the inspector, the menus and the shortcuts act on; N and Shift+N step through the
  designs on it. What draws over a canvas, its outlines, the zoom bar, the drawing toolbar, extensions' layers and the
  console docked under it, shows on the canvas in focus. What's selected is the project's, so it stays as lenses come
  and go.
- **The lens bar works as links do in a browser.** A click shows a lens in the tab in focus, and Ctrl+click or a middle
  click opens it in a new tab; one that's open is revealed where it is. Clicking the lens in front hides or shows the
  left panel. Ctrl and a lens's number shows it, Ctrl+1 for Pages and Ctrl+2 for Screens. The arrow keys, Home and End
  move between lenses. Right-clicking one offers Show, Open in new tab, Split right and Close.
- **Tabs** drag onto another group's tabs to join them, or onto a canvas's side to split. A tab's close button, or a
  middle click, closes it, the last one too.
- **Every tab closed empties the window:** the left panel and the inspector go, and the canvas's place says No lens
  open, with how to show one. A canvas closes with its tab, or when another lens takes its tab's place, and showing its
  lens again draws it afresh where its camera was.
- **Lenses stay in the main window** until the desktop app has lens windows (PAR-1247): the menus don't offer Move to
  new window, and a tab let go outside the window stays where it was.
- **The panels are the window's panel layout,** so the lens bar, Show Layers and the other panel commands, the View
  menu's panel toggle and extensions show and hide the same panels. A hidden panel is gone rather than left as a rail of
  its tabs, as in the exploration, and the lens bar or a panel command brings it back.
- **Component previews** are made for as long as the project is open, whether or not Screens shows: once a canvas has
  come up, a lens closed doesn't hold them back as a canvas still loading does.

Code: `OpenProject.tsx` renders `LensWorkspace` with `appLenses`, in `lenses/app-lenses.ts`, opening on Screens;
`lenses/screens.tsx` is Screens (`screensLens`) and `lenses/pages.tsx` Pages (`pagesLens`). Their canvases are
`ProjectCanvas` in `lenses/project-canvas.tsx`, which reads the open project through `OpenProjectContext`, gives the
project its editor while its lens is in focus, and renders `CanvasEditor` with what it `draws` (`drawsDesign`, with
`isRoutePage` in `canvas/route-pages.ts`). `CanvasEditor` keeps each canvas's camera as it goes (`keptCameras`). The
shell is `lenses/LensWorkspace.tsx`, with `LensBar.tsx`, `LensTab.tsx`, `GroupActions.tsx` and `dock-adapter.ts`, the
one file that calls Dockview; its decisions are `@parity-app/lenses`'s. Without a `popoutUrl`, `LensWorkspace` keeps
lenses in its window.

### Pages, a lens of its own (PAR-1244)

The app's routes and their pages have a lens of their own, Pages, as
[lens-layout.md](proposals/lens-layout.md#lenses-down-the-left) has it. Screens no longer draws them.

- **Its canvas** draws each page as a screen, laid out in the router's tree with the lines between them and layouts
  without a page as groups around theirs, as Screens drew them before. It's drawn the first time Pages shows, so opening
  a project on Screens loads no page. Shown again after another lens took its place, it's where its camera was, with
  what was selected still selected. A page is drawn from the app's code, so the canvas has no drawing toolbar: F and T
  leave it on Move and select, and files dropped on it make nothing.
- **Selecting stays on its canvas.** Select all, Select inverse and Select matching select only pages, and N steps
  through them; layers kept selected from another lens's canvas count as nothing selected. A router's Show routes, and
  its route count in the status bar, show Pages with its Layers, and an extension's `navigate.reveal` and `zoomTo` show
  the lens whose canvas draws the node first. A page selected while another lens shows, from Search, shows Pages in that
  lens's place with the page in view; a design selected while Pages shows, or made from its menu, shows Screens the same
  way. A canvas showing part of what's selected never narrows it for the others.
- **Its Layers** lists the routes and their pages' layers, as Layers' Routes group did; Screens' Layers no longer has
  that group. Selecting a page there or on its canvas shows it in the inspector. Layers is its panel's only tab, so
  asking for another from Pages, such as Show Components (Alt+2), the status bar's tokens, or an extension's tab, shows
  Screens in its place with that tab open.
- **The inspector** shows the selected page as before: its header, its path params as props, its route and Export. Under
  them, its links: the components it places that have a board, each showing its board in Screens, selected, with Show
  beside at the row's end splitting Screens to the right. A page places its route's components, whose boards Screens
  doesn't draw, so the example's pages show none yet; links to screens and tables wait for what relates them
  (Components, PAR-1245, and Data, PAR-40).

### A project with no Parity file opens on a Home screen (PAR-561)

Opening a folder or project that has no `.par` file yet opens on a screen named Home, for the app's `/` route. It draws
the component that renders the app there, live, in the project's primary mode with a phone's mode beside it: Desktop
Light and Mobile Light with the default modes. There's no empty canvas to start from.

- **What renders `/`:** the page for it, by its router's file names: Next's `app/page`, also inside a route group such
  as `app/(marketing)/page`, or an `index` in a `pages` or `routes` folder, a route file's default export over its other
  parts. Without one, it's the `App` component that Vite's and Create React App's templates mount, by its export name or
  as `App.tsx`'s default export. When there are several, the one in the fewest folders wins. A library's component is
  never it.
- **Without either,** the screen is a padded page headed Home, as New screen starts one.
- **The page fills the screen:** the component sits in the screen's root layout, unpadded, on the theme's background.
- **The mode beside the primary one** is the first mode on a phone, preferring one whose theme and other options match
  the primary mode's, so Mobile Light comes before Mobile Dark beside Desktop Light. Beside a phone's primary mode it's
  a laptop's or desktop's. With no mode on the other kind of device, the screen shows the primary mode alone.
- **Opening writes nothing.** The Home screen opens as if the main project file held it: there's nothing to undo or
  save, and the folder is left as it was. The file is written with the first change, Home screen included. Closed
  without a change, the project opens on a new Home screen next time.
- **Only a project with no project file gets one.** One whose designs were all deleted opens with none. A file that
  can't be read stops the project opening (see below), so there's never a Home screen to write over it.
- **A blank project from the scaffolder (PAR-284) has no project file either,** so it opens on a Home screen the same
  way.

Code: `openingDesigns`, `homeScreen` and `homeComponent` in `packages/editor/src/home.ts` (`@parity-app/editor`), which
`createSession` in `apps/desktop/src/renderer/workspace.ts` calls with what `project.open` gave it. In Storybook, Parity
/ App / Blank project opens on the Home screen. The stories of Layers with nothing in it open `designless`, a project
whose file holds no designs.

Tests: `packages/editor/src/home.test.ts` (13: a Home screen in the main file of a project with none, and a project's
own files as they are; the screen drawing `App` with Mobile Light beside Desktop Light, a padded page headed Home with

alone; and what renders `/`: Next's, a `pages` folder's and a `routes` folder's page over `App`, a route group's, a
route file's default export, `App` by export or file and the nearest one, never a library's, and nothing). Gap:
`createSession` calling it has no automated test.

### Each page of the app as a screen, in its tree (PAR-1076)

An app whose router Parity reads (TanStack Router, see support.md) opens with each of its pages as a screen above the
designs, laid out as the router's tree, top down. A page is a route the router draws on its own. A layout's index that
draws stands for the layout, so the layout's other pages hang from it: the example's App, at `/`, holds Pricing,
Projects, Project detail and Settings. Each page is centered over the pages under it, and pages side by side go by path.
A screen is named for the component its route draws, else its path.

- **Layouts without a page.** A layout with no page of its own, because it has no index or its index draws nothing and
  only redirects, is a group around its pages instead of a page: the example's `/settings` index only redirects to
  Profile, so Settings is a dashed, rounded outline around Billing and Profile, side by side on its level, 48 canvas
  pixels in from its sides. Its header, at a title's size, shows the layout icon, its name and path, and a chip with
  where its index redirects, Profile, whose tooltip says "Redirects to Profile"; clicking the chip selects Profile. The
  line from the page above ends at the group's top edge. Clicking the header selects the group, whose outline turns
  solid in the page color, and brings forward its line up to App. Its panel shows the layout icon, its name and Layout,
  then what the router says of its layout route, read-only: its path, file and component, where its index redirects as a
  link that selects that page, and whether it loads data or can redirect. It has no frame of its own, so no modes or
  Export (`PageGroupPanel`). The selection holds the group's layout route by `NodeRef`, as an extension's
  `parity.selection.set` does too (PAR-1092), so selecting a design takes the selection from it. A group is named for
  its path's last part, or for its component when its path is its parent's, as a pathless layout's is. The group's
  outline is drawn round its pages where they are now, so it follows a page that's moved.
- **Any router, in Parity's terms (PAR-1132).** The tree, names and URLs come from each route's kind (root, layout,
  group or page) and its URL as segments (fixed, param, catch-all, optional catch-all), which the router's extension
  translates from its own syntax (`ProjectRoute` and `RouteSegment` in `packages/core/src/routes.ts`; `segmentsOf` in
  `packages/extension-tanstack-router/src/routes.ts`). A route's path, as the router writes it, is only shown: in a
  layer's name and the route panel. A parallel route's slot and an intercepting route aren't drawn yet, so the tree
  leaves them out with the routes inside them (`drawnRoute`). Tests: `packages/core/src/routes.test.ts`, and
  `packages/editor/src/route-boards.test.ts`, "leaves out a parallel route's slot and an intercepting route".
- **Where a route redirects.** The TanStack Router adapter reads where a route always redirects from its route options:
  the first statement of its `beforeLoad`, else its `loader`, when it's `throw redirect({ to: "…" })`. A redirect inside
  an `if` is a sometimes, and doesn't count.
- **Where a page lands.** A page's frozen copy says where its page landed, from the page runtime's snapshot, and a live
  board's page says where it went with `page.ready` and `page.moved`. When the path isn't the page's own, ignoring a
  trailing slash, an amber "Lands on /x" warning shows under the page's board, lined up with its left edge and a few
  screen pixels below at any zoom, sized as a frame's caption is, so a redirect Parity couldn't read still shows. Its
  row in Layers shows an amber warning too, whose tooltip says where. The example's Dashboard is behind a sign-in check
  in its `beforeLoad`, so it lands on `/login` until someone logs in.

- **Layers.** Layers lists the app's pages under Routes, before Screens and Frames, in their tree: each page under the
  page above it, App, then Pricing, Projects, Project detail and Settings a level in. A layout group is a folder with
  the layout icon and, at its right, where its index redirects, holding its pages: Settings holds Billing and Profile.
  It's open until it's closed with its arrow, or Left and Right; clicking it selects its layout route, by `NodeRef`
  (PAR-1092), which selects its group on the canvas and brings the group into view. Each icon at the end of a row has a
  tooltip saying what it means: where a layout redirects, where a page lands, that a component fails to draw, that a
  layer changes in the state shown or at some screen sizes, and what it's locked with. A search lists the pages flat.
  Component designs are listed in the Components panel. A page shows the route icon, in Layers and on its title, and its
  title shows its route's path under its name; selecting it shows its route's path, params, file and component, and
  whether it loads data or can redirect, read-only. Its layers are what each route that draws it draws, the root's
  outermost, each inside the one before as it draws at that route's outlet, as children passed to it: Billing's are
  RootLayout, SettingsLayout, Billing. Each shows as the component its route draws, with the component's icon and color,
  and its panel shows its route too; a route that names no component, as a redirecting index, shows as a route, named
  for its path. What each component draws inside comes with React's tree (step 4).
- **Names.** A page is named for its component in words, as ProjectDetail is "Project detail", else its path's last
  part, as the `/settings` index is "Settings", else Home.
- **Lines.** A dashed line runs from the middle of each page's bottom edge to the middle of the top edge of each page
  under it. It curves across above the lower page's title, 8 screen pixels short of it, and drops straight down from
  there to the board, behind the title, whose name and path sit on the canvas's own color. Pages side by side share a
  level, so a line only ever passes behind the title of the page it leads to, at any zoom: zoomed out, where a title
  takes more of the canvas, the curve turns down higher. Once a title reaches up to the page above, the line curves all
  the way down. Its dashes flow slowly down the tree, at any zoom, so the tree shows which way it runs. Lines are faint
  until a page is selected or hovered, on the canvas or in Layers: then its way up to the top of the tree and its lines
  to the pages right under it come forward in the page color, drawn over the rest. Selecting Billing brings forward
  Billing's line and Settings' group's, and selecting Settings' group brings forward its line up to App. A line into a
  group curves straight down to the group's top, since a group's header isn't a title it passes behind. The lines are
  drawn from where the boards are now, so they follow a page that's moved, and they sit behind every board.
- **The app draws it.** A page's frames show a frozen copy of the app's own page at the page's URL (below), which ran in
  a document of its own, so the app's router, layouts, loaders and redirects ran as they do in a browser: `/settings`
  shows Profile, where its index redirects. With the Interact tool, a board goes live: the page itself, over its copy
  (below). Designs are still drawn by the guest in Parity's window. A frame loads under a name of its project's own,
  `http://p<hash>.localhost:<port>` (`pageFrameUrl`), which Chromium reaches on the loopback address and runs in a
  process of its own, so one project's pages never share a process with another's (PAR-1260). Vite and Next's
  development server accept those names as they come; the webpack-compatible builders' server lets the page's own name
  load its chunks (`isPageOrigin`).
- **A value for each param, in Props.** Selecting a page shows its route's path params under Props, before Route, as
  text fields, each with the param's name as its placeholder. A value draws the page at that URL (`samplePath` with the
  view's `params`, in `routePageUrl`), written as a URL writes it; an unset one is the param's name, and an unset
  catch-all is empty, so `/projects/$projectId` opens on `/projects/projectId` until it's given one. The URL comes from
  the route's segments, which its router's extension gives in Parity's terms (`RouteSegment` in
  `packages/core/src/routes.ts`), so no router's syntax is read outside its extension (PAR-1132). The values are how the
  canvas shows the page, never the app's code, and are kept with what else is set on it (see Kept in the project file,
  below). Tried in a development build: Project detail opened on `/projects/projectId`, which the example says it can't
  find, and setting ProjectId to `atlas` drew the Atlas project at `/projects/atlas`. Code: `samplePath` in
  `packages/editor/src/route-boards.ts`, the view's `params` in `packages/core/src/document.ts`, and `RouteProps` in
  `apps/desktop/src/renderer/chrome/RoutePanel.tsx`. Tests: `packages/editor/src/route-boards.test.ts`, "fills a param
  with the value given for it, written as a URL writes it".
- **Kept in the project file.** What's set on a design drawn from code, a page's, a component board's or a story's, is
  kept in the project's file under `codeDesigns`, by the design's key, and set on it again when its code draws it next
  time the project opens: what it shows (its view: modes, their order and scales, and a page's params) and, for a story,
  the sizes tried on its layers. Nothing else of it is saved, and nothing is written to the app's code. A design missing
  for now, such as a story whose file fails, keeps what it had. Tried in a development build: setting Project detail's
  ProjectId to `atlas` and saving wrote it under `codeDesigns`, and after reloading the window the page opened on
  `/projects/atlas` again, with nothing unsaved. Code: `codeDesignSettings` and `withCodeDesignSettings` in
  `packages/editor/src/tried-size.ts`, `codeDesigns` in `packages/core/src/document.ts`, and `withCodeDesigns` and
  `keepCodeDesigns` in `apps/desktop/src/renderer/canvas/code-designs.ts`. Tests:
  `packages/editor/src/tried-size.test.ts`, "what's set on a design drawn from code". Gaps: a story's kept modes and
  tried sizes weren't tried in the app, and `code-designs.ts` has no unit test.
- **Never saved.** Page screens are laid out from the routes each time the project opens, in a design file of their own
  that's never written. They can be selected and moved, but a move isn't kept. A copy takes no pointer, so the canvas
  pans and selects over it. With the Interact tool, a press makes the board live (below), and clicking Pricing in App's
  live page takes it to `/pricing`. Otherwise it's inert, as a design's frame is, so Tab on the canvas never goes into
  the page and leaves the canvas's keys there (`keyboard.e2e.ts`, "keys outside Interact").
- **The page runtime (PAR-1260).** The builder serves the page runtime first in the app's page
  (`@parity-app/page-runtime`, as [proposals/route-frames.md](proposals/route-frames.md) sets out): Vite as a module
  script at the top of `<head>`, the webpack-compatible builders as the first module of each of the app's entries, and
  Next from its `instrumentation-client`, which every client entry runs before React. With it come the extensions' page
  modules: the router's, which moves the app with its own router (TanStack Router's reads `window.__TSR_ROUTER__`, React
  Router's `window.__reactRouterDataRouter` or the router library mode made, and Next's `window.next.router`), and the
  renderer's, which says when the app has hydrated (React's installs a minimal `__REACT_DEVTOOLS_GLOBAL_HOOK__` and
  waits for the first commit to the app's root, never to Next's development overlay). The frame's name is `parity:` and
  JSON with the protocol's version, the frame's id, Parity's origin, and the mode and window it opens in. The runtime
  posts its hello to Parity's origin only, and Parity checks the hello's origin and source, hands it a `MessagePort` and
  runs `@parity-app/channel` on it (`usePageChannel`). A page that reloads says hello again and gets a new port. Once
  the app has hydrated, the page says where it is and which router can move it; with no hydration module, once it has
  loaded and its DOM has been quiet for 150 ms. After that it says where it moves by itself, by its router or by its
  address, and that someone used it, at most once a second. Anywhere other than a frame Parity named, the runtime does
  nothing.
- **Each router's page module (PAR-1260, PAR-1265).** A router's move is done once the new page is in the DOM, not when
  the router first says so. TanStack Router's waits for the router to resolve where it ended. React Router's waits for a
  commit, heard on `__REACT_DEVTOOLS_GLOBAL_HOOK__`, of the tree holding the `RouterProvider` given the app's router,
  with the new location in its state. `RouterProvider` hands React the new state in a transition, and a route that
  suspends keeps the old page, with no commit, until it's ready; another root's commit, as an embedded widget's, doesn't
  count. Where its hooks can't be read, that tree committing counts. Without a hook it waits for the page's first
  change, or 100 ms without one. Next's App Router writes the address with the tree it commits, a new one each commit,
  so its module waits for a write carrying a new tree, redirected anywhere, and not for the app's own writes, which
  carry none or a copy of the last, and the Pages Router's `push` resolves once the new page has committed. Library mode
  puts no router on the page's window, so Vite and the webpack-compatible builders serve the app's own imports of
  `react-router` through Parity's module (`pageWraps` in the manifest), which re-exports React Router and hands what
  `createBrowserRouter` and `createHashRouter` make to `window.__parityDataRouter`. That module gets the app's own copy
  of React Router, and packages' own imports are left alone. A page whose router isn't found, as with React Router's
  `<BrowserRouter>`, says so in `page.ready`, and is moved only by loading it at the route.
- **Modes reach the page, without a reload.** The frame opens in its mode, and when the mode changes Parity sends it
  with `mode.set`: the runtime puts the mode's classes and attributes on `<html>`, takes off the last mode's, and
  answers `prefers-color-scheme` with the mode's scheme, telling the app's queries when the answer changes. An app that
  follows the system's theme, as the example's theme provider does, follows the mode's: in Desktop Light the page's
  `<html>` is `light` with a white background. An app that keeps its own choice of theme, in `localStorage`, uses that,
  and its page frames share it, since they're one origin.
- **As tall as the page.** Each viewport's frame is as wide as its viewport and as tall as its page, with no scrollbar:
  App, whose page runs 49px past a 1280 × 800 window, is 1280 × 849. The runtime hides the page's scrollbar, so the page
  lays out at the mode's whole width, and says how tall the page is (`page.height`) whenever that changes while its
  window is the mode's (Desktop 800, Tablet 1024, Mobile 844). The frame grows to it but never shrinks below the window.
  It measures only in the mode's window because a page with a section as tall as the window grows with the frame,
  without end. A mode that changes takes the frame back to its window until the page says how tall it is there. So a
  page that changes after it first draws, as a live page does, keeps the height it first had. A frame given a height of
  its own keeps it and scrolls, but page frames have no resize handles yet.
- **Frozen copies (PAR-1262).** Each route board's frame shows a frozen copy of its page, as
  [proposals/route-frames.md](proposals/route-frames.md) sets out. One frame per project, the freezer, makes them: it's
  parked in Parity's window at 1% of its size, where Chromium still lays it out, and for each route that needs a copy,
  nearest the view first, it loads the route fresh, then for each mode its boards draw (or each markup group, below)
  sets the mode (`mode.set`), sizes itself to the mode's window and asks for a snapshot (`snapshot.take`) once the page
  has been quiet for 150 ms, at most 3 s. The page runtime answers with the body's tree as plain data, URLs made
  absolute and form state written in as attributes, `<html>`'s classes and attributes without the mode's, the page's
  height, where it landed, and its stylesheets by content hash. Parity asks for the sheets it hasn't got (`sheets.get`),
  and main fetches a sheet on another host, such as a web font's, over `https:` (`pageSheet`). The snapshot is parsed
  with its schema, which refuses a page past 50,000 elements, 256 deep or 8 MB of text, and passed through
  `sanitizePage` and `sanitizeRoot`. The board builds it with `buildCopy` in a shadow root from `prepareFrame`, with a
  custom element registry of its own, so the guest's definitions don't upgrade its elements; each sheet goes through
  `sanitizeSheet` and `prepareCanvasCss` once and is shared by every copy. `<html>`'s classes and attributes go on the
  frame's host and on an element around the body stand-in, as tall as the mode's window as the page's root was,
  `<body>`'s on the stand-in, and the mode's on the host and the stand-in. A web component's open shadow root comes with
  its own styles, and a canvas comes as a picture at the size it was drawn. A copy is as tall as its page in the mode's
  window, unless the board has a height of its own, and it's inert, so nothing in it takes focus or follows a link.
  Until its copy or picture comes, a placeholder stands in at the window's height.
- **Pictures (PAR-1200).** A board small on screen or away from the view shows a picture of its copy instead of the copy
  itself, as [proposals/route-frames.md](proposals/route-frames.md) sets out. It turns into its copy once it's near the
  view and wider than 440 screen pixels, and back into its picture once it's narrower than 360 or leaves the view
  (`boardTier`), so a board resting between the two doesn't flip. The tier follows the camera as it zooms. A board with
  no copy yet stays a picture. The picture is taken in an offscreen render window, which builds the copy with the same
  `buildCopy` and `prepareFrame` as the board (`mountCopy`), at the mode's width and the page's full height, sanitized
  again first, with its lazy images loading at once, and captures it at a quarter of the board's size. No page loads
  there, and viewport units measure the mode's window, so a section sized in `svh` keeps its height. Pictures are kept
  on disk as frames' bitmaps are, named by the project, the route's path and query, the mode as it resolved, the state
  and the scale (`pageBitmapName`), with the page's trace inside: what the builder says the route's files and its
  parents' load, Parity's scan of their imports, what mounts the app and its imports outside the routes (`appEntries`)
  with the root's `index.html`, the stylesheets, the shared config and the `public` folder, or every file under the
  route's folder and those directly in each folder above it, such as a template, and those folders' parallel slots for
  Next, or the whole project where the builder can't say or the page redirected or drew its not-found or error page
  (`pageTraceFiles`). A picture whose traced files changed after its copy's page started loading is kept without a
  trace, so it stands in, stale. A kept trace stops holding when a file it lists changes or a file the page's trace
  would now list is added, such as a new layout. A copy standing in from another mode's snapshot until it's checked
  isn't captured. A kept picture shows as soon as the project opens, before the freezer has made the copies again; it's
  checked again with each new copy, and one whose trace doesn't hold shows until it's captured again. A capture that
  fails is tried again after 2 s, doubling up to 16 s. Route boards ask for no design bitmaps of their own.
- **Selecting inside a copy.** A copy's frame is registered under its page's design with its mode and state, and its
  elements have ids from their place in the body (`0.3.1`), which `buildCopy`'s `DrawnNodes` maps, so clicking and
  double-clicking select inside a copy as in a design's frame, with the element's outline, name and spacing. Layers
  lists what the copy draws inside the route that draws the page: Pricing's are RootLayout, Pricing, then `div`,
  `header` and `main`. Those layers are made again with each freeze and kept in the window (`copyLayers`), never in the
  project's document. They're made without styles; the Design panel reads an element's computed style when it shows it
  (`withCopyStyle`).
- **Copies follow the code (PAR-1264).** The project service's watcher tells the window which of the app's files changed
  (`project.filesChanged`), 250 ms after the last, leaving out hidden folders such as `.git` and `.next`, installed
  packages, builders' output at the project's root (a `build` folder deeper down can be the app's), `.par` files and
  TypeScript's build records (`pageSourceChange`). A copy is kept by its route, mode and state (`CopyKey`) and the mode
  as drawn, so duplicated designs at other widths or themes keep their own, with the trace it was made from.
- **Only a route's own files refreeze its copies (PAR-1298).** After each snapshot the freezer asks the project service
  for the copy's trace (`pages.trace`), the same files as its picture's (`pageTrace`): the route's chain, what the
  builder says it loads, Parity's scan of their imports, what mounts the app, the stylesheets, the shared config and the
  `public` folder. A change to a file in it makes the copy stale; another route's file leaves it as it is. Where the
  router names routes by folder, as Next's, a file added in the route's folder, directly in a folder above it or in
  their parallel slots counts too, as a new layout or loading file does. Where the builder can't say, for a page that
  redirected or drew its not-found or error page, and when the service doesn't answer, the trace is the whole project,
  so any change, an added file included, makes the copy stale. A copy one of whose files changed while its page loaded
  is frozen again at once. A stale copy stays shown until the freezer has a new one, nearest the view first. Modes whose
  snapshots drew the same markup form a markup group: a route frozen again takes one snapshot per group, which every
  copy in the group shows at once with its own height, and each other mode is checked with a snapshot of its own once
  nothing is missing or stale. Two states of a route share a copy. A page that loads again while it's frozen says hello
  again with the same id: the freezer replaces its channel, waits for it to be ready and takes the snapshot again, three
  times at most. With the Interact tool, when the app's files change, a project's live page under Vite or a
  webpack-compatible builder, which keeps the modules it loaded, is loaded again where it is (`page.reload`, or at its
  last location when it doesn't answer), and a frame still going live once it's live; its spares are closed and opened
  again. A page whose router is Next's takes Next's hot updates in place. The webpack-compatible builders' pages no
  longer poll and reload themselves.
- **Style previews in copies.** Token values edited and not yet saved show in every copy, in the same frame as in the
  design frames: the page's own stylesheets hold the saved values, so the project's previewed values go into one sheet
  every copy of its routes adopts after its own (`tokenPreviewCss`). A default value is declared on the copy's host and
  body, except where the class of a theme the token has a value of its own in is, and a theme's value where its class
  is: Desktop Dark keeps `primary`'s dark value, and takes an edited `radius`, which has none. A theme's value given,
  saved and undone shows the token's default there. A theme turned on by an attribute, such as `[data-theme="dark"]`,
  counts as its class does (the guest's `themeAttributes`). The pool's live and spare pages get them over their channel
  (`preview.set`), when they connect and as they change, into a sheet their snapshots never list. A copy's layer has its
  style fields on: a value being typed or scrubbed shows in every copy of the page, goes when the edit ends, and is
  never saved (`StylePreview`, `previewRules` with `changedOnly` and `important`). Its fields start from the copy's
  drawn style (`withCopyStyles`), and the preview wins over the page's inline styles. Its other fields stay read-only.
- **Live boards (PAR-1263).** With the Interact tool, a route board can be the app's own page, as
  [proposals/route-frames.md](proposals/route-frames.md) sets out. Each project keeps two spare frames per window while
  Interact is on: the app's page in an iframe on its builder's origin, in a layer in the canvas's page space above the
  boards (`LiveLayer`), parked in the view at its mode's full size, drawn at 1% and taking no pointer, where Chromium
  still lays it out. They load at the app's root and move with the app's own router to the routes of the boards in view,
  nearest the middle first (`planPool`), and park again 250 ms after the view stops moving. With no page router they're
  loaded at the route they're for. Resting the pointer on a board for 80 ms sends a spare to its route and mode. A press
  on a board takes the quickest frame (`pickLive`): the one warming on it, a spare on its route, any spare sent there,
  one still loading, or a new frame at the route. The page is put over the board, one mode window tall, scaled with the
  board, and engaged: it takes the pointer, the wheel scrolls it and keys go to it. That press only does that; the next
  one lands on the page. The runtime passes back what's Parity's when the page didn't take it: Ctrl or Cmd with the
  wheel, or a pinch, zooms the canvas at that point (`page.zoom`), and Escape and Ctrl or Cmd shortcuts, except the ones
  that edit or move through text, reach Parity's document (`page.key`). Escape the page didn't handle, a press anywhere
  outside the page and leaving Interact disengage it: the frame takes no pointer again, stays live, and focus comes back
  to Parity's document, since a page with focus keeps getting keys. Hovering a live board never takes the wheel.
  Disengaged, the live window sits over the part of its board in view, with the page scrolled to match (`page.scroll`,
  `liveWindowTop`); engaged, the page's own scrolling moves it down its board (`page.scrolled`). While a board is live
  its copy hides its fixed and sticky elements, so a fixed header shows once. A link to another of the app's routes
  moves the live page, and the board says where it went, as a redirect does. A navigation off the builder's origin is
  stopped in main (`pageFrameGuard`, on `will-frame-navigate` and `will-redirect`), and the board says "Tried to open"
  with the host. Live ends when another board goes live or the board has been out of view for 10 s, and its frame is
  closed, never reused. The freezer waits while the live page is in use, 2 s after each `page.used`, and while the pool
  refills, 1.5 s after a board goes live, since a project's frames share one process. A window that isn't focused keeps
  no spares. `routeFrame.live` says how a board went live and how long it took, and `routeFrame.miss` that no spare was
  there.
- **When the page process fails.** A project's pages share one renderer process. When it closes the freezer's channel or
  a request misses its deadline, the freezer starts again after 1 s, then 5 s, then 30 s, and after three failures in
  two minutes it stops for that project; boards keep the copies they have.
- **Bundled up front.** The builder's server scans `index.html` with the components, so what only the app's entry
  imports, such as its router, is bundled before the first page asks for it. Bundled later, it was bundled again under
  the pages, which then had two copies of React.

Tried in a development build on the example project, opened cold: six page screens in two levels, Billing and Profile in
Settings' group with its Profile chip, four lines from App to Pricing, Projects, Project detail and the group, each page
showing its page, with no errors; the lines' dashes moved from each page toward the pages under it. Layers listed App,
its four pages a level in, and Billing and Profile in the Settings folder; clicking the folder selected the group on the
canvas. Moving Pricing's page with `history.replaceState` showed "Lands on /pricing/annual" under its frame. Dashboard's
frame drew the login page, and its row in Layers showed the warning, with "Lands on /login" on hover.

Frozen copies were tried in a development build on the example project (PAR-1262): all eight page boards showed their
copies within a few seconds of opening, each with the page's own fonts and styles, no iframe left once the freezer was
done, and nothing in a copy with a script, frame or handler. Pricing's copy matched its page at 1280 wide; Layers listed
its `div`, `header` and `main` inside Pricing, selecting `main` there outlined it on the canvas at 1280 × 751 with its
Region panel, and double-clicking the pricing cards on the canvas selected their `div`, named in its outline, with its
read styles in the Design panel. Dashboard's row in Layers kept its warning from its copy's landing on `/login`. Mobile
and dark modes and a failing page process weren't tried in the app.

Code changes and previews were tried in a development build on the example project (PAR-1264). Editing PlanCard, the
Pricing route's component, on disk ("a month" to "per month, billed yearly") showed in Pricing's copy 4.4 s after the
save, and putting it back showed again. With Desktop Dark turned on too, both copies changed in the same frame, 7.6 s
after the save, from the one snapshot of their markup group. With the Interact tool, the same edit loaded Pricing's page
again with the change. Setting `primary`'s Light value in the Tokens panel turned the Choose Team button in Pricing's
copy blue in the same frame, while Desktop Dark's kept its own value; the page drawn with the Interact tool showed it
too, and again after it loaded again for the code change. Undo put both copies back. A page that loads again while
frozen, and a webpack-compatible project, weren't tried in the app.

Copies refrozen by their own page's trace were tried in a development build on the example project (PAR-1298). After the
freezer had frozen all seven routes, editing Profile's heading on disk froze Profile again, with Dashboard, which lands
on `/login`, and Project detail, whose sample param draws its not-found page, as both take the whole project. Pricing,
Login, Projects and Billing stayed as they were. Putting the heading back froze the same three again. A Next.js
project's added layout wasn't tried in the app.

Live boards were tried in a development build on the example project (PAR-1263). With Interact, two spares parked in the
view; resting on Pricing marked it ready, and a press made it live and engaged in 94 ms, the page exactly over its copy
and holding focus. Ctrl and the wheel over it zoomed the canvas from 55% to about 61%. Escape disengaged it, with focus
back in Parity's document; a press on it engaged it again, and a press in Layers disengaged it. On App, whose page runs
49px past its window, the wheel scrolled the page by 49px and the live window moved down the board with it. Clicking
Pricing in App's live page took it to `/pricing`, with "Lands on /pricing" under the board and in Layers, and sending it
to `https://example.com/` was stopped, with "Tried to open example.com". Pressing Login ended App's live page and made
Login's live. Panned away, App's live page, live again by then, closed after 10 s out of view; leaving Interact closed
the spares, and coming back opened two again. A Ctrl shortcut passed back, an unfocused window and a page without a page
router weren't tried.

Pictures were tried in a development build on the example project (PAR-1200): zoomed out to 8% and 25%, all eight page
boards showed pictures of their pages, with no page frame left once the freezer was done. Zooming in to 50% turned the
board in view into its copy, and the boards outside the view stayed pictures. Zooming back out to 30% kept the copy, and
20% turned it back into a picture. After reloading the window, all eight pictures showed from disk within 9 s of the
reload, while the freezer was still on its first route. Copacker wasn't tried: its pages are server-rendered by TanStack
Start, and the page runtime doesn't reach them yet, so its freezer gets no hello and none of its boards get a copy.

The page runtime was tried in a development build on the example project (PAR-1260): all eight page frames loaded under
the project's own `p….localhost` name, each with `window.parityFrame`, the mode's classes and no scrollbar, and App's
frame grew to 849 from the page's `page.height`. Dashboard's warning came from its `page.ready`. Setting Desktop Light's
theme to Dark in the Modes panel turned every page dark without loading it again, its `prefers-color-scheme` query
answering dark, and back. Setting its viewport to Mobile made App's frame 390 wide and 893 tall, measured in the 390 ×
844 window, and back to 849. A page that reloaded by itself connected again and took both changes.

### Each of the project's components on a board of its own (read-only viewer, step 8)

The project opens with a board for each of its own components, below the pages and above the designs. Library components
and pages aren't on boards, and neither are providers or the parts the Components panel hides. There's a row for each
group in the panel: the UI kit's by file, as Card with CardHeader and CardTitle, and the rest of the app's by folder.

- **Drawn from the code.** The guest draws each component as inserting it would place it. A component a story draws
  takes that story's args first, the first story's for each component, so Plan card draws with its name, price and
  features rather than failing without them. Any other required prop gets its default or its first option, and a
  component that takes children gets its own name as text. It starts without samples and takes them once the props have
  been read from the component's types, a moment after the project opens. The board hugs the component with 2px around
  it, so nothing at its edges is cut off, and has no fill, so the component sits on the canvas. Its title shows the
  component's icon and its name, without its file. At 100% a component is its own size: the example's Button is 65.7 ×
  32, as in a browser.
- **Inside the parents a part needs.** A part that fails for want of a parent, as AvatarImage needs Avatar and
  TabsTrigger needs TabsList inside Tabs, is drawn again inside the next parents to try (`nextBoardParents`), until it
  draws: first the component its error names, then the components of its file whose names begin its own, outermost, then
  the rest of its file. A parent that gets it further is kept, and one that doesn't, or fails itself, is dropped. A
  parent that hides it, as an inactive TabsContent hides what's in it, counts as drawing nothing, so the search goes on,
  and comes back to it when no parent shows it: an AvatarImage with no picture shows nothing anywhere. It stops after 12
  tries. Layers still opens straight to the part's layers, without its parents.
- **In the component's color.** A board is selected, outlined and titled in the component purple, with its size under it
  in the same color, though it's a frame.
- **Only the project's own.** A component from a library, or from a dependency in `node_modules`, gets no board; it's
  still listed in the Components panel.
- **Listed in Layers and the Components panel.** Layers lists the boards under Components, after Routes and Screens.
  Pressing one of the project's components in the Components panel selects and shows its board. Dragging it still
  inserts it, and pressing a library's component still adds it where the selection is.
- **Every layer inside.** A board is the component, so its row in Layers opens straight to what the component draws,
  with no layer for the board's padding or for the component around it: Card opens to `card` and its Text. Each element
  it draws is a layer, read from the page each time the board is drawn live. `img`, `svg` and `canvas` are images,
  `video` a video, and a text element (`p`, `span`, headings, `strong`, `em`, `label`, `a` and the like) with only text
  in it is text. Any other element, a `div` or a `button` with its text in it, is a layout with its text as a layer
  inside. A layer is named for its `data-slot`, as shadcn names its parts, else its role, else its tag. Its styles are
  what it's drawn with: its size, a layout's direction, gap, padding and alignment, its fill, border, corners and
  opacity, and a text's type. Selecting one outlines its element on the canvas.
- **Each layer is its element's type.** A layer read from an element keeps its tag and the attributes that say what it
  is, and `describeElement` in `@parity-app/layer-types` gives its type: its icon in Layers and in its panel's header,
  and its family's color, as an orange Button for a `button` or a blue Layout for a `div` (Layers/Element types in
  Storybook has the whole mapping). The header calls it by its type, with its role, input type or tag beside it, and it
  has no Make component.
- **Read-only panel.** A selected board's panel shows its file and the export it's drawn from. Under Props, it lists the
  props the component declares and its variants, each with its options or type and its default. The attributes and
  handlers it passes through to its element aren't listed. A layer inside it shows its type's sections: first the ones
  its attributes fill (`panelData`), as Link with its `href` and target, a Checkbox with its name and whether it's
  checked, or a video's Source and Playback, leaving out one with nothing set; then its text, for text; then the style
  sections its type has, as a Button's Typography, Size, Appearance, Fill and Stroke. A layer of a page shows the Design
  tab's sections with its values. None of them edits it.
- **Never saved.** The boards are laid out each time the project opens, in a design file of their own that's never
  written. Neither a move, the width a board is drawn at, nor its layers being read marks the project unsaved. Pages and
  boards are left out of what Parity keeps to restore after a crash.
- **Not yet.** A part that shows only when chosen, as TabsContent does, draws nothing. A page's layers don't show what
  its components draw inside, since the page is the app's own document on another origin.

Tried in a development build on the example project. Its own UI kit showed 36 boards in 10 rows under the page tree.
Pressing CardTitle in the Components panel selected its board, with `src/components/ui/card.tsx` and its export in the
panel. Button's panel listed its variant and size options and `asChild` = false. Reopening left nothing unsaved. Card's
row opened to `card` and Text; selecting `card` outlined it and showed its size, padding and fill, greyed. Button's row
opened to `button` with the orange Button icon, and its panel's header said Button, with Typography, Size, Fill, Stroke
and Appearance; Input's `input` was a Text field. With the search, AvatarImage and AvatarFallback drew inside Avatar,
TabsList and TabsContent inside Tabs, and TabsTrigger inside TabsList inside Tabs, and the canvas showed no errors;
TabsList's board fit to 71 × 36, all in purple.

### Each story file as a story design (read-only viewer)

The project opens with a design for each of its Storybook story files, listed in Layers under Stories, after Screens,
and laid out down a column left of everything else on the canvas, each as far below the last as its stories need. A
story file is a design of its own kind, a story (core's `containerKinds`), which nothing places as an instance and
nothing converts to another kind. Its stories are its states, a row each on its board, every one shown at first.

- **Listed as Storybook lists them.** Under Stories, each part of a file's title but its last is a folder, as
  Storybook's sidebar nests them, and the file is listed by its last part, as `Button` in UI, under Storybook's teal
  square split in four, with how many stories it has. Its stories are the layers inside it, each a teal bookmark named
  for itself, as `Outline`. Folders start closed; selecting a story file on the canvas opens the folders it's in. A
  click opens or closes a folder. The arrow keys move through folders and rows alike: Right opens a folder or goes into
  it, Left closes it or goes up to the folder above, and Enter or Space opens or closes it. A search opens every folder
  with something found in it and leaves out the rest. The adapter says which folders each file is in
  (`ImportedScreen.folders`); Layers draws any adapter's that way.
- **Read through an extension.** Storybook's extension, through its entities provider (PAR-1095), reads each
  `*.stories.*` file's CSF: the meta's `title`, `component` and `args`, and each story's `name` and `args`. The service
  runs every adapter whose tool the project depends on when it opens, and the files come in the project's info, one
  `ImportedScreen` each.
- **Each story its own layers, shown alone in its state.** Each story is its meta's component, a library's or the
  project's own, with the meta's args and its own over them as props, inside bounds of its own named for the story
  (`bounds:Outline` around `story:Outline`). Each state hides every other story's bounds, so a row draws its own story
  only, and a story with its own `render` keeps its own tree. The file's root is padded and on the page's background, as
  Storybook's default layout draws a story, and hugs it (core's `fitsContent`): each story's preview is as wide as it
  draws in that mode, measured for each story apart (`frames`, by `Outline/desktop`, see `fittedKey`) and not saved,
  while the story lays out in the mode's whole window, so its media queries and viewport units read the mode's width, as
  in Storybook's canvas. Once a story's preview is measured, it sleeps on its bitmap zoomed far out as any frame does;
  before PAR-1106 it was looked for by its mode's viewport alone, so it never counted as measured and never slept
  (`sleeping.e2e.ts`).
- **Its props, modes and sizes in the Design panel.** Selecting a story file shows its header, then Props, the args of
  the story picked, the row of the preview picked last, else the first (`pickedStory`), which edit and are written back
  as below, then Modes: its board draws each story's preview in each mode it shows, across. A story file's view, its
  modes, scales, previews and which stories show, is kept in the project's file (see Kept in the project file).
- **Resized to test.** Dragging a story's bounds, or any layer's that takes a size, sets a width or height on it, and
  the preview fits the new size while the window stays the mode's, to see how the story responds. Size, with Reset size,
  then shows at the end of the Design panel, and puts every layer back at the size the story's file draws it
  (`withoutTriedSize`, against `drawnStory`), leaving its args. A tried size is never written to the story's file; it's
  kept in the project's file until it's reset. A component that doesn't take a style, as PlanCard, can't be sized
  itself, so its bounds are there to drag.
- **Or its own `render`.** A story that renders itself, with its own `render`, the meta's, or as a function (CSF 2),
  draws that function with its args as props. The adapter gives it as a source of its own (`ProjectEntities.sources`, as
  `Invite.render` in the story's file), which the guest loads as it loads a component, and its layer takes the story's
  name.
- **Args written back.** The props of what a story draws are its args, and they edit as any component's do. Saving sends
  the stories' design file to the service (`entities.save`), which hands each file whose layers or states changed to the
  adapter that imported it (`EntitiesAdapter.export`). Storybook's extension writes each story's props, with what its
  state sets over them, as the args that differ from the meta's into the story's `args` in its file, keeping code there,
  such as a function, as it's written.
- **Otherwise read-only.** The rest of a story file's design is Storybook's to lay out: its other layers and sections
  show their values without editing them, and nothing else of it is saved.
- **Named and coloured by its provider** (PAR-1131). What Layers lists story files under, what their states are called
  (a board's menu, a row's count, the Design panel's "Story, read from its Storybook file") and the colour of their
  icons come from the entities provider's manifest (`group`, `states` and `color`), which Parity keeps with the imported
  screens (`ProjectEntities.looks`). Each provider's story files get a Layers group of their own. Nothing in Parity's
  own code names Storybook; without a manifest colour, story files take a screen's blue.
- **Not yet.** A story's decorators, loaders and the `context` its `render` is given aren't applied. A story file added
  while the project is open shows once it's opened again. A story that's a function, or whose args are a constant, isn't
  written to, nor can a story take away an arg its meta gives. A screen can't yet be saved as a new story.

Tried in a development build on the example project: Layers listed Badge, Button, Card and Plan card under Stories, Plan
card in App. Plan card's board drew Default, Popular and Team and Business a row each, each preview as wide as its own
story, Team and Business's two cards wider than the others. Props showed the picked story's args, and setting Popular's
Price to $32 and saving wrote `price: "$32"` into the Popular story's args alone, beside `popular: true`. Not tried this
time: dragging a story's bounds and Reset size, and a story file shown in several modes.

### Stale views are pruned

A design's view names modes, states and route params, and what it names can go: a mode taken out of the project, a story
taken out of its file, a route's param renamed. Nothing stale is left to show in a menu or pile up in the file.

- **When a mode is taken away in Parity,** the same step takes it out of every design's view: the modes it shows, its
  order, its scales and the previews in it (`prunedDocument`, from `setModes` in `packages/multiplayer/src/callers.ts`).
  Undo puts both back.
- **When the project opens,** every design's view is pruned against the project's modes, its own states and, for a page
  of the app, its route's params (`withPrunedView`), so what changed outside Parity, in the project file or the app's
  code, goes too. What's kept for designs drawn from code (`codeDesigns`) loses the entry of a design its file no longer
  draws, as a story file deleted, unless nothing of that file was drawn this time, as when its tool couldn't be read
  (`openCodeDesigns`). The file loses what was pruned at its next save.
- **A layer that's gone** loses its tried size the same way, since what's kept is read again from the design as it is.

`packages/multiplayer/src/callers.ts`; `openCodeDesigns` in `apps/desktop/src/renderer/canvas/code-designs.ts` and
`routeParams` in `route-pages.ts`, run from `createSession` in `workspace.ts`. Tests:
`packages/editor/src/prune-view.test.ts` (modes gone wherever named, states gone as a story taken out, a screen's
